[L2]   "content": "# Whirligig R/Q Engine: rolling sphere, gimbals, two equations, Curvy_Lisa

**Version:** experimental v0.1, 11 October 2026  
**Status:** SANDBOXED engineering reconstruction. Mathematical/procedural tool, not a proof of a physical isomorphism.

This is a working, configurable **two-equation** mechanism drawn from the historical R/Q / Great Annulum / W_obble / W_iggle / Curvy_Lisa description, together with the archived continuous Navier–Stokes Whirligig Python predecessor. It generates equation curves on a sphere, carries them inside a rolling ball constrained by a torus, uses two genuine orthogonal gimbal hinges to select curve endpoints, constructs the R–Q crossbar and a rotation-minimizing plane perpendicular to it, then intersects a rotating pen ray with the **actual torus quartic** to generate Curvy_Lisa.

**Source provenance:**
- [*FINDING THE DONUT*, pp. 23–27](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/_AUTO_EXTRACTED_TEXT/FINDING%20THE%20DONUT%20(nolat).txt), March 2026.
- [*THE_WHIRLIGIG*](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/HsH-SAT%20Roundup%203/THE_WHIRLIGIG.txt).
- [Existing continuous NS Whirligig source](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS/30SEP26_DUMP/continuous_ns_whirligig_solver%20%281%29.py), independently specifying the sphere's moving contact frame, Bishop connector, torus-wall ray casting, and a Navier–Stokes test setup.
- [*WHIRLIGIG -- REDEFINING SUCCESS*](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/WHIRLIGIG%20--%20REDEFINING%20SUCCESS.txt): a **constructive existence** goal for a back hallway, not a demand for one unique universal derivative.
- Original source distinguishes 3D mechanical toy geometry from actual four-dimensional systems. This code does too.

## Run

```bash
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python whirligig.py --input example_equations.json --out output --search
python plot_mechanics.py --input example_equations.json --out mechanics_snapshot.png --gif rolling_whirligig.gif
python validate_mapping.py --input example_equations.json --out mapping_validation.json
python -m pytest -q
```

`--input` is optional: a two-harmonic-pair demonstration is built in.

## Input equation adapters

Two independent specs are supplied as `R` and `Q` in a JSON file. Every adapter records its representation choice, physical units remain those of the caller, and original numerical coordinates are preserved apart from the sphere carrier. **No universal faithful parameterization exists for arbitrary symbolic equations without specifying a solution branch, observables, and a parameter interval.** Accordingly the tool supports:

| Kind | Example | What is done | Limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| `expression` | `0.5*cos(2*t)+0.1*sin(5*t)` | Scalar function encoded reversibly in sphere latitude; azimuth is `t` | Functions must be finite on the interval. Periodicity tested, not fabricated |
| `parametric` | `{"components":["cos(t)","sin(t)"]}` | 2D trajectory via reversible stereographic embedding; 3D trajectory radialized with magnitude preserved separately | 3D radial projection loses magnitude in its sphere output |
| `implicit` | `x*x/2.25+y*y-1=0` written as `x*x/2.25+y*y-1` | Extract largest closed real zero contour and stereographically lift | Grid approximate; must set bounding box and a suitable branch |
| `ode` | `{"rhs":["y","-x"],"initial":[1,0]}` | Numerically integrates a 1–3 dimensional ODE and embeds the path | May not close; only specified initial-value solution is represented |
| `sampled` | `{"path":"path.csv"}` | Arclength-resamples a closed 2D/3D numeric curve | Intended for PDE/GR/field equations solved upstream; refuses open CSV curves |

Expression parsing is AST-restricted: arithmetic and common NumPy scalar mathematical functions only. No `eval()`, attribute access, user code import, or arbitrary shell expression execution.

For a PDE, differential geometry equation, non-Euclidean metric, or symbolic Schwarzschild geodesic, **first choose a solution and chart** and pass the resulting parametric/CSV path. This prevents smuggling an arbitrary metric into a falsely universal polar-projection routine. Keep the full source equation and domain as metadata outside the low-dimensional carrier.

## Exact selected-contact rolling law

Let the torus have major radius `R` and tube/minor radius `a`. Let the sphere have radius `b<a` and travel on a center circle of radius

\[
\rho=R+a-b,\qquad C(\psi)=\rho(\cos\psi,\sin\psi,0).
\]

The selected contact on the outer equator is

\[
P(\psi)=(R+a)(\cos\psi,\sin\psi,0)=C+b\mathbf e_r.
\]

For rolling without slip at this **isolated chosen point**, the laboratory angular velocity obeys

\[
\boldsymbol\omega=-\frac{\rho}{b}\dot\psi\mathbf e_z,
\quad \dot C+\boldsymbol\omega\times(b\mathbf e_r)=0.
\]

Define the Great-Annulum body contact angle

\[
\gamma(\psi)=\frac{R+a}{b}\psi.
\]

Let `W(ψ)` be the orthonormal world frame `(e_r,e_phi,e_z)` and `B(γ)` the body-frame triad `(r_annulus,t_annulus,n_annulus)`. The **actual orientation** is

\[
\mathcal Q(\psi)=W(\psi)B(\gamma)^T\in SO(3).
\]

`P=C+Q b r_annulus` is tested point by point. A whole-revolution orientation closes when the contact gearing `g=(R+a)/b` is integral. The historical *even multiple* condition is satisfied by choosing `g=6` by default:

- `R=1.6`, `a=0.55`, `b=(R+a)/6=0.358333...`, `rho=1.791666...`.
- A five-point fourth-order finite-difference check of the no-slip velocity converges to zero under grid refinement, while the underlying analytic identity is exact.
- With `b=a` (the originally described limiting sphere size), ball and torus tube share a nonisolated meridional contact set. The program **can render that mode** when `allow_degenerate_contact=true`, but explicitly does **not certify unique-contact rolling**; imposing no slip at every contact point would be overconstrained.

## Gimbal, connector and pen

The input R endpoint is acted on by an internal `Ry(pitch)` hinge; the Q endpoint by an independent `Rx(roll)` hinge. Their axes are perpendicular **by exact construction**. Hinge angles use integer-period rotations with optional sinusoidal modulations. The sphere's physical `SO(3)` rotation is separate from these **internal coordinate controls**. The two endpoints are transported into the lab frame with the exact `Q(ψ)` orientation above.

`W_obble=(R_world+Q_world)/2` is the connector midpoint, and `W_iggle` is the plane perpendicular to the connector. A minimal-rotation Bishop frame supplies its two orthonormal axes. The pen rotates in that plane. Its **first forward** intersection with the torus is found by solving the torus implicit quartic and selecting its smallest positive real root, not by approximating a torus-looking curve.

Optional `align_source_anchors` rotates one source curve **by a single rigid SO(3) alignment**, mapping an off-phase point and tangent on Q to a point and tangent on R. This is a transparent representation intervention, **not an isomorphism proof**, and it is logged with the alignment matrix and both residuals.

An optional Bishop-holonomy correction adjusts the pen's phase around the full circuit. The correction is recorded, and may be disabled: the program does not silently assert that an uncompensated trace must close.

## Results and automatic smoothness search

The `--search` scan varies **four even annulum gear ratios**, pen rotation rates, and independently chosen gimbal rotations. It preserves **all sixty** ranked candidates in `ranked_candidates.json`, including failures; it also saves the selected best candidate's full reproducible arrays, metrics and precision geometry figures. The ranking favors:

- valid mechanical contact, SO(3) orientation and torus quartic intersections;
- nondegenerate sphere/tube clearance;
- both input-equation closures and full orientation closure;
- C¹ seam closure, low curvature variation, low curvature percentile, low high-frequency Fourier tail.

These smoothness thresholds are **engineering filters**, not physical selection laws. C² seam mismatch is reported separately, and smooth candidates must not be mistaken for solutions to the source equations on the other side of their chosen projections. Explicit held-out source-equation residual tests are required before a proposed back hallway is accepted.

For the supplied synthetic two-harmonic pair with independently aligned anchors:

| Diagnostic | Observed |
|---|---:|
| selected contact velocity (analytic) | `0.0` |
| selected contact velocity, 128 samples | `2.14823e-4` |
| selected contact velocity, 256 samples | `1.34990e-5` |
| selected contact velocity, 512 samples | `8.44822e-7` |
| ball-frame closure | `1.73e-15` |
| torus implicit residual | `8.53e-14` |
| Curvy_Lisa positional seam | `8.55e-16` |
| C¹ seam (tangent difference) | `0.00117` |
| R anchor point and tangent gaps | `2.89e-17`, `1.42e-16` |
| response to +1% R amplitude | `0.00287` RMS output shift |
| response to +1% Q amplitude | `0.00903` RMS output shift |

The tests include intentionally nonperiodic inputs and nonintegral rolling gear, both of which must fail the relevant closure checks. Thirteen automated tests passed in the first checked build.

## Files

- `whirligig.py`: generalized two-equation 3D mechanical engine, parsers, closure checks, finite-clearance rolling, search.
- `ui4d.py`: separate, exact six-plane `SO(4)` Universal Indicatrix representation using `y(s)=r(s)R(s)x0`; **not yet coupled to 3D rigid-ball mechanics**.
- `plot_mechanics.py`: precision-drawn sphere/gimbal/annulum/connector/pen figures and optional GIF.
- `validate_mapping.py`: finite-difference grid convergence and independent source-equation perturbations.
- `test_whirligig.py`: 11 regression/negative tests.
- `example_equations.json`: two independent scalar formula inputs with optional anchor alignment.
- `example_ode_vs_implicit.json`: harmonic oscillator versus an ellipse equation.
- `example_historical_limit.json`: equal-radius historical rendering with explicit degeneracy diagnostic.
- `demo/`, `aligned_demo/`: retained 60-run candidate sweeps and selected-best numerical arrays and plots.

## Remaining work

1. **Historic Great Annulum:** source says a self-intersecting annulum with antipodal self-tangent, but does not give its analytic curve. This release makes an explicit great-circle choice. Recover and test the intended self-intersecting annulum before calling this exact historical reconstruction.
2. **4D rolling/gimbal lift:** the sphere/torus apparatus implements the explicitly described **3D toy version**. The separate `ui4d.py` provides its honest SO(4) representation layer, not a fabricated four-dimensional contact geometry.
3. **Joint dynamical derivations:** embedding an equation into a polar curve is not equivalent to deriving an invariant relation from two different equations. Implement input-specific residual or observable maps and compare against held-out predictions in both sectors.
4. **Continuous optimization:** current candidate search is discrete, not a variational or interval-arithmetic global search. Upgrade with constrained smooth optimization, holonomy loops, singularity branch resolution, and complexity/energy budgets.
5. **Metrology and units:** use dimensionless toy geometry until source physical scales and constraints are specified. Do not import GR coefficients into an assumed definition of the engine.

**Research handling:** mathematical apparatus should be assessed independently of speculative framing; no physical claim is inferred from geometric representability alone. Attribution: SAT/H(s)H user and archive research, with original sources linked above; free reuse with citation to source where appropriate.

## 1. Original full apparatus, not the reduced experiment
Nathan's own description in FINDING THE DONUT pp. 23–27 (many explicitly revised ideas; prefer his latest per-paragraph geometry, keep rejected preceding proposals as provenance):
1. Start with equation solution curves R and Q (not necessarily literal algebraic formulas as input). Represent them in a common controlled, perhaps 4D, curve space using Universal Indicatrix (UI). Ideally loops with a shared intersection `i_r` and equatorial intersection `i_q`. Original language changes from two concentric spheres to curves on one sphere/torus, then a sphere rolling inside a torus; do not silently unify incompatible intermediate drafts.
2. Two rotating gimbal planes connected at right-angle `i_r O i_q`, with independent axes, explicit phase and frame transport. A variable-length cord `i_r i_q`, midpoint `W_obble`, perpendicular `W_iggle` plane, and rotating ray/vector `V`.
3. `GrAnn` (Great Annulum) with special self-intersection `GrAnn_Omph` at `i_r` and antipodal tangency `GrAnn_t_ipode`; its exact geometric realization is UNDER-SPECIFIED by the prose. The sphere is constrained to a torus (“The Donut”), minor radius equal to sphere radius, major radius arbitrary; `P_ivot` on `TorOuRad` and GrAnn, with `Donomphulon` on `TorInCirc` and `BigRad` across the torus section. Sphere rotates/rolls along toroidal track. Each outer-torus circuit must complete an even integer multiple of circuits around GrAnn (an explicit archived kinematic condition).
4. `Curvy_Lisa` = the **first forward intersection of the moving vector V with the torus surface**, a geometric trace identified with Q-with-respect-to-R. It is NOT merely the chord midpoint, a 2D Lissajous plot, or concatenating the two input curves.
5. Nathan explicitly calls this “just the three-dimensional toy version”; an SO(4)/4D lift is additional engineering, not automatically solved by a 3D torus simulation.
6. Nathan stresses keeping tangent/holonomy consistency at crossover: a *smooth* transition needs matching tangents; matching coordinate-frame curvature alone is not enough.

### Mechanical subtleties requiring honest engineering
- A sphere of radius exactly equal to the torus **tube radius** is a limiting contact configuration: contact can be degenerate rather than a unique single point. Separate: **historical exact-radius mode** (kinematics with constraint diagnostics) vs **finite-clearance single-contact physical rolling mode**. Do not advertise full no-slip at an extended contact locus.
- Existing solver uses `annulus_parameter= -[(torus_major_radius + ball_radius)/ball_radius]·psi`. Verify inside/outside rolling sign, contact path, and actual no-slip with `v_contact = Cdot+ω×r_contact` evaluated against the stationary wall; do NOT infer physical no-slip from the prescribed ratio. Independently check body rotation orthogonality, pin coincidence, connector perpendicularity, ray intersection, and closure of **position + tangent + full orientation/holonomy**. Matching plotted endpoints alone is insufficient.
- Hard-coded gimbals must specify axis order, handedness, SO(3) or SO(4) composition, units, and reference frames. Need independent tests that frame orthonormality and determinant stay at 1, and that no interpolated frame flips by 180°.
- Closure cannot be manufactured by joining endpoints or by forcing an arbitrary Fourier cutoff. Record winding ratios, near-return, residual and initial-condition mismatch. If rolling frequency is irrational relative to torus winding, honest result may be nonclosure.

## 2. Proposed engineering contract (next immediate work)
**Deliver runnable package**, not just a plan:
- Reuse/fork archived `continuous_ns_whirligig_solver (1).py`, retaining its detailed audit outputs. Put new code in `WORKSPACES/COMMON/WHIRLIGIG_ENGINE/` (or a versioned sandbox) and commit actual Python, README, tests, and test results.
- API: `EquationAdapter` takes 1) explicit parametric solution curve; 2) ODE or Hamiltonian system plus IVP and numerical integrator; 3) manual sampled periodic path with units/uncertainty; 4) possibly PDE/field encodings with a FULL reversible/round-trip map, as in the NS solver. No promise that *any* unsolved implicit equation admits a canonical automatic compact spherical encoding.
- `SphereProjector` maps normalized variables into north/south hemisphere using explicit invertible latitude transform when information-preserving (or report lossy). Preserve equation identity, state dimension, singularities and scale metadata. Add tests for numerical round-trip and parameter monotonicity, not just image similarity.
- `GimbalMechanism` contains sphere position, body orientation, independently rotating planes, annulum, `W_obble/W_iggle`, connector and its Bishop frame, forward-ray pen. `RollingContact` checks the actual contact geometry and no-slip residual.
- `TorusIntersection` uses quartic ray/implicit torus or bracketing with verified first-forward root; handle tangent roots and branch switches. Validate implicit surface F(x)=0 for **every** accepted point.
- `ClosureAnalyzer` computes endpoint, tangent, full frame, holonomy, contact and periodicity residuals separately. “Closed loop” only upon meeting agreed numerical tolerance and refinement convergence; report winding numbers.
- `SmoothPathSearch` starts with multiple integer winding combinations and bounded gimbal/phase parameters; optimize for smoothness (e.g. integrated squared curvature / bending, curvature derivative and cusp penalty), while placing geometry, correct projection, no-slip, closure and equation residuals FIRST as constraints, not terms that can cheaply be violated. Keep the Pareto-ranked survivors AND rejected candidates with reasons. Watch for reparameterization-dependent bending scores and fake “better” paths created by slowing the parameter.
- Output: parameter JSON, normalized input curves, provenance, solver settings, two-target mapping trial, full 4D/3D frame arrays, output curve, diagnostics, figures and executable regression tests. Compare with original NS test fields and a simple exact loop pair as independent fixtures.
- Acceptance gate: documented input inversion accuracy, SO(3) orthogonality and det(+1), contact condition, actual rolling/no-slip residual for finite-clearance case, first wall-hit residual, sufficient smoothness, closure including rotation, and converged results across sampling densities. Rejected nonclosing paths ARE valid diagnostic outputs.

### First suggested fixtures
A) Identity: same known closed curve supplied to both ports, verify all frames and single-contact rolling, no spurious “isomorphism.” B) Distinct rational-winding curves with known analytic closure, test recovered full orientation. C) Incommensurate frequencies deliberately showing nonclosure. D) Existing archived Navier–Stokes A and B velocity fields via reversible spectral encoding. **Only after engine passes these**: Kepler negative-energy → S³ regularization → hydrogen hidden SO(4), then Schwarzschild relativistic perturbation.

## 3. Scope of previous October Clifford torus paper
- [SANDBOXED Clifford-torus elastic paper](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/COMMON/SANDBOXED_PAPERS/WHIRLIGIG_CLIFFORD_TORUS_ELASTIC_BACK_HALLWAY_2026-10-08.md) already committed. This is a model-specific mode response, not a discovered fundamental-force coupling.
- SO(4) rotation symmetry of UI; S³≅SU(2) as manifolds; `Spin(4) ≅ SU(2)_L×SU(2)_R`; Clifford T² subset S³ is NOT a subgroup of SU(2) (SU(2) maximal torus U(1)). Keep separate from old conjectural “Schwarzschild ↔ SO(4)/SU(2)/SU(4)” identification.
- [Implementation scope audit](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/COMMON/SANDBOXED_PAPERS/WHIRLIGIG_IMPLEMENTATION_SCOPE_2026-10-09.md).
- Review requests [Meridian #23](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/issues/23), [Mercer #24](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/issues/24); **at time of handoff both open, no peer-review replies**, only author's v0.2 update comments. Why or why not?” Do not claim those colleagues are actively working or have reviewed unless actual comments appear.
- Earlier conversation linked generated local ZIP/PDF/scripts, but **the only verified persistent GitHub artifacts are the two Markdown files linked above**. Do not assume the local ZIP/scripts were committed to GitHub or remain accessible in a new conversation. The new engine needs its own repository code.

## 4. GR–QM “Lagrangian Closure” document: verified numerical/mechanical issues
Source: [2026 LAGRANGIAN CLOSURE + QM-GR ISOMORPHISM.txt](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS/MOSTLY_EARLY_NLM/2026%20LAGRANGIAN%20CLOSURE%20%2B%20QM-GR%20ISOMORPHISM.txt), 155,539 chars, 3,205 lines; internal content dated April 8, 2026, **not necessarily chronological**; much is AI/NotebookLM output. Separate calculations from narratorial praise and assertions of “proof.”

The S³ Laplacian spectrum is mathematically standard; the *hinge identity* is a proposed unproven physical identification. “Common frequency” `ω⁴=−2λ_s r_h²/κ` for positive parameters yields negative RHS and has no mode-number dependence to imply `ω~1/n`. Deriving independent hydrogen absolute energy yielded ≈−4.46e−21 J vs target −2.18e−18 J (≈489-fold). Later text claims this was closed using a fine-structure ratio but no independently adequate chain demonstrated. Reusing observed α is not zero-input prediction.
- Perihelion calculation states correct GR result `6πGM/[a(1−e²)c²]` after dimensional scaling; does not derive the coefficient from the Whirligig’s Euler–Lagrange equation. Gravitational mass sourcing needs to be implemented, not inferred by analogy to S³ geodesics.

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import cumulative_trapezoid
from scipy.interpolate import CubicSpline
def check_rolling(A=0.22, R=1.65, b=.55, N=1500):
    tt=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,12001)
    def g_of_t(t):
        lat=A*np.sin(2*t)
        return np.array([np.cos(lat)*np.cos(t),np.cos(lat)*np.sin(t),np.sin(lat)]).T
    gtab=g_of_t(tt)
    deriv=np.gradient(gtab,tt,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    spd=np.linalg.norm(deriv,axis=1)
    u=cumulative_trapezoid(spd,tt,initial=0)
    lenG=u[-1]
    # One psi-interval staying within one grann cycle; no seam issues
    psi=np.linspace(.1,1.5,N)
    gear=(R+b)/b
    ui=gear*psi
    theta=np.interp(ui,u,tt)
    gr=g_of_t(theta)
    dt=np.gradient(gr,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    tan=dt/np.linalg.norm(dt,axis=1)[:,None]
    normal=np.cross(gr,tan)
    B=np.stack([gr,tan,normal],axis=2) # columns
    er=np.array([np.cos(psi),np.sin(psi),np.zeros_like(psi)]).T
    et=np.array([-np.sin(psi),np.cos(psi),np.zeros_like(psi)]).T
    ez=np.zeros_like(er);ez[:,2]=1.
    W=np.stack([er,et,ez],axis=2)
    QQ=W@np.transpose(B,(0,2,1))
    C=R*er
    cp=np.gradient(C,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    qdot=np.gradient(QQ,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    skew=qdot@np.transpose(QQ,(0,2,1))
    omega=np.stack([skew[:,2,1],skew[:,0,2],skew[:,1,0]],axis=1)
    slip=cp+np.cross(omega,b*er)
    # curv of g via arclength
    tand=np.gradient(tan,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)/gear
    kg=np.sum(tand*normal,axis=1)
    residual=np.linalg.norm(omega-( -gear*kg[:,None]*er+ (1-gear)*ez),axis=1)
    inward=omega*er
    return {'geodesic_length':lenG,'contact_slip_mid_max':float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(slip[10:-10],axis=1))),
           'expected_lambda_spin_range':(float(np.min(-gear*kg)),float(np.max(-gear*kg))),

            'spin_range':(float(np.min(np.sum(omega*er,axis=1))),float(np.max(np.sum(omega*er,axis=1)))),
            'kg_range':(kg.min(),kg.max())}

    def g_of_t(t):
        lat=A*np.sin(2*t)
        return np.array([np.cos(lat)*np.cos(t),np.cos(lat)*np.sin(t),np.sin(lat)]).T
    gtab=g_of_t(tt)
    deriv=np.gradient(gtab,tt,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    spd=np.linalg.norm(deriv,axis=1)
    u=cumulative_trapezoid(spd,tt,initial=0)
    lenG=u[-1]
    # One psi-interval staying within one grann cycle; no seam issues
    psi=np.linspace(.1,1.5,N)
    gear=(R+b)/b
    ui=gear*psi
    theta=np.interp(ui,u,tt)
    gr=g_of_t(theta)
    dt=np.gradient(gr,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    tan=dt/np.linalg.norm(dt,axis=1)[:,None]
    normal=np.cross(gr,tan)
    B=np.stack([gr,tan,normal],axis=2) # columns
    er=np.array([np.cos(psi),np.sin(psi),np.zeros_like(psi)]).T
    et=np.array([-np.sin(psi),np.cos(psi),np.zeros_like(psi)]).T
    ez=np.zeros_like(er);ez[:,2]=1.
    W=np.stack([er,et,ez],axis=2)
    QQ=W@np.transpose(B,(0,2,1))
    C=R*er
    cp=np.gradient(C,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    qdot=np.gradient(QQ,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    skew=qdot@np.transpose(QQ,(0,2,1))
    omega=np.stack([skew[:,2,1],skew[:,0,2],skew[:,1,0]],axis=1)
    slip=cp+np.cross(omega,b*er)

    tand=np.gradient(tan,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)/gear
    kg=np.sum(tand*normal,axis=1)
    residual=np.linalg.norm(omega-( -gear*kg[:,None]*er+ (1-gear)*ez),axis=1)
    inward=omega*er
    return {'geodesic_length':lenG,'contact_slip_mid_max':float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(slip[10:-10],axis=1))),

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import cumulative_trapezoid
from scipy.interpolate import PchipInterpolator

def cam_curve(theta, amplitude):
    th=np.asarray(theta)
    beta=amplitude*np.sin(2*th)
    bp=2*amplitude*np.cos(2*th)
    bpp=-4*amplitude*np.sin(2*th)
    er=np.stack([np.cos(th),np.sin(th),np.zeros_like(th)],axis=-1)
    et=np.stack([-np.sin(th),np.cos(th),np.zeros_like(th)],axis=-1)
    ez=np.array([0,0,1.])
    g=np.cos(beta)[...,None]*er+np.sin(beta)[...,None]*ez
    gp=- (bp*np.sin(beta))[...,None]*er+np.cos(beta)[...,None]*et+(bp*np.cos(beta))[...,None]*ez
    gpp=-(bpp*np.sin(beta)+bp**2*np.cos(beta)+np.cos(beta))[...,None]*er-2*(bp*np.sin(beta))[...,None]*et+(bpp*np.cos(beta)-bp**2*np.sin(beta))[...,None]*ez
    speed=np.linalg.norm(gp,axis=-1)
    t=gp/speed[...,None]
    w=np.cross(g,t)
    kg=np.sum(np.cross(gp,gpp)*g,axis=-1)/speed**3
    return g,t,w,speed,kg

def calculate(amplitude=0.22, sphere_radius=.55, windings=4, n=1800, major=None):
    theta_grid=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,25001)
    speed=cam_curve(theta_grid,amplitude)[3]
    u=cumulative_trapezoid(speed,theta_grid,initial=0)
    L=u[-1]
    if major is None: major=sphere_radius*(windings*L/(2*np.pi)-1)
    gear=(major+sphere_radius)/sphere_radius
    psi=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,n+1)
    u_param=gear*psi
    if np.max(u_param)>windings*L+0.0001: raise RuntimeError("more than windings")
    theta_of_u=PchipInterpolator(u,theta_grid)
    theta=theta_of_u(np.minimum(u_param,windings*L)) # up to the exact endpoint
    g,t,w,speed,kg=cam_curve(theta,amplitude)
    B=np.stack([g,t,w],axis=-1)
    er=np.stack([np.cos(psi),np.sin(psi),np.zeros_like(psi)],axis=1)
    et=np.stack([-np.sin(psi),np.cos(psi),np.zeros_like(psi)],axis=1)
    ez=np.zeros_like(er);ez[:,2]=1
    W=np.stack([er,et,ez],axis=-1)
    Q=W@np.swapaxes(B,1,2)
    C=major*er
    P=C+sphere_radius*np.einsum("nij,nj->ni",Q,g)
    desired=(major+sphere_radius)*er
    pivot_err=np.max(np.linalg.norm(P-desired,axis=1))
    torus_err=np.max(np.abs((np.hypot(P[:,0],P[:,1])-major)**2+P[:,2]**2-sphere_radius**2))
    ortho_err=np.max(np.abs(np.swapaxes(Q,1,2)@Q-np.eye(3)))
    orientation_seam=np.linalg.norm(Q[0]-Q[-1])
    # omega formula from moving Darboux frames
    omega=(-gear*kg)[:,None]*er+(1-gear)*ez
    slip=major*et+np.cross(omega,sphere_radius*er)
    slip_max=np.max(np.linalg.norm(slip,axis=1))
    # independently finite differences
    dq=np.gradient(Q,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    dC=np.gradient(C,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    A=dq@np.swapaxes(Q,1,2)
    w_fd=np.stack([A[:,2,1],A[:,0,2],A[:,1,0]],axis=1)
    slip_fd=dC+np.cross(w_fd,sphere_radius*er)
    slip_fd_max=np.max(np.linalg.norm(slip_fd[5:-5],axis=1))
    return {"L":L,"major":major,"gear":gear,"windings":gear*2*np.pi/L,
            "curvature_range":(kg.min(),kg.max()),"spin_range":(-gear*kg).min(), "spin_max":(-gear*kg).max(),
            "pivot_err":pivot_err,"torus_err":torus_err,
            "ortho_err":ortho_err,"orientation_seam":orientation_seam,"slip_max":slip_max,
            "fd_slip_mid":slip_fd_max, "Q":Q,"psi":psi,"kg":kg}
results = {}
for A in [0,.08,.22]:
    results[A]=calculate(amplitude=A)
    print(A,{k:v for k,v in results[A].items() if k not in ("Q","psi","kg")})

def calculate2(amplitude=0.22,b=.55,m=4,n=1800):
    theta_grid=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,25001)
    Lcurve=cam_curve(theta_grid,amplitude)[3]
    arclen=cumulative_trapezoid(Lcurve,theta_grid,initial=0)
    L=arclen[-1]; major=b*(m*L/(2*np.pi)-1)
    gear=(major+b)/b
    psi=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,n+1)
    u=gear*psi
    cycles=np.floor(u/L+1e-12)
    rem=u-cycles*L
    rem=np.clip(rem,0,L)
    th=PchipInterpolator(arclen,theta_grid)(rem)+2*np.pi*cycles
    g,t,w,_,kg=cam_curve(th,amplitude)
    B=np.stack([g,t,w],axis=2)
    er=np.stack([np.cos(psi),np.sin(psi),np.zeros_like(psi)],axis=1)
    et=np.stack([-np.sin(psi),np.cos(psi),np.zeros_like(psi)],axis=1)
    ez=np.zeros_like(er);ez[:,2]=1
    W=np.stack([er,et,ez],axis=2)
    Q=W@np.transpose(B,(0,2,1))
    C=major*er
    P=C+b*np.einsum("nij,nj->ni",Q,g)
    vanalytic=(-gear*kg)[:,None]*er + (1-gear)*ez
    sla=major*et+np.cross(vanalytic,b*er)
    dq=np.gradient(Q,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    dC=np.gradient(C,psi,axis=0,edge_order=2)
    AA=dq@np.swapaxes(Q,1,2)
    wd=np.stack([AA[:,2,1],AA[:,0,2],AA[:,1,0]],axis=1)
    slfd=dC+np.cross(wd,b*er)
    return dict(L=L,major=major,gear=gear,windings=gear*2*np.pi/L,
        curvature=(float(kg.min()),float(kg.max())),spin=(float((-gear*kg).min()),float((-gear*kg).max())),

        orientation_seam=float(np.linalg.norm(Q[0]-Q[-1])),
        contact_gap=float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(P-(major+b)*er,axis=1))),
        sphere_orientation=Q,psi=psi,kg=kg)

Let torus major radius R0, equal torus tube and sphere radius b=a, and torus orbital angle psi. Fix a selected outer-wall point P=(R0+b)e_r and C=R0 e_r. Rolling at that point demands:

    C_dot + omega cross (b e_r) = 0.

from pathlib import Path
source = r'''#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Sandboxed GrAnn material-cam rolling reconstruction.

This is a nominated-contact SO(3) mechanism, not the historical self-crossing
Great Annulum or a globally no-slip b=a torus-sphere contact.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import cumulative_trapezoid
from scipy.interpolate import PchipInterpolator


def latitude_cam(theta, amplitude):
    """Unit-sphere material path with closed nonzero geodesic curvature."""
    theta = np.asarray(theta, dtype=float)
    beta = amplitude * np.sin(2 * theta)
    db = 2 * amplitude * np.cos(2 * theta)
    ddb = -4 * amplitude * np.sin(2 * theta)
    er = np.stack((np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta), np.zeros_like(theta)), axis=-1)
    et = np.stack((-np.sin(theta), np.cos(theta), np.zeros_like(theta)), axis=-1)
    ez = np.array([0., 0., 1.])
    g = np.cos(beta)[..., None] * er + np.sin(beta)[..., None] * ez
    gp = (-db * np.sin(beta))[..., None] * er + np.cos(beta)[..., None] * et + (db * np.cos(beta))[..., None] * ez
    gpp = (-(ddb * np.sin(beta) + db**2 * np.cos(beta) + np.cos(beta)))[..., None] * er - (2 * db * np.sin(beta))[..., None] * et + (ddb * np.cos(beta) - db**2 * np.sin(beta))[..., None] * ez
    speed = np.linalg.norm(gp, axis=-1)
    tangent = gp / speed[..., None]
    h = np.cross(g, tangent)
    kg = np.sum(g * np.cross(gp, gpp), axis=-1) / speed**3
    return g, tangent, h, speed, kg


def solve_cam(amplitude=0.22, radius=0.55, even_cycles=4, steps=2400,
              major=None, grid=25001):
    if radius <= 0 or even_cycles < 2 or even_cycles % 2:
        raise ValueError("Need positive radius and positive even GrAnn cycles")
    th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, grid)
    speed = latitude_cam(th, amplitude)[3]
    arc = cumulative_trapezoid(speed, th, initial=0)
    length = float(arc[-1])
    if major is None:
        major = radius * (even_cycles*length/(2*np.pi) - 1)
    if major <= radius:
        raise ValueError("Selected major radius does not give a ring torus")
    gear = (major+radius)/radius
    psi = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, steps+1)
    s = gear*psi
    lap = np.floor(s/length + 1e-12)
    remainder = np.clip(s-lap*length, 0, length)
    theta = PchipInterpolator(arc, th)(remainder) + 2*np.pi*lap
    g,t,h,_,kg = latitude_cam(theta, amplitude)
    B = np.stack((g,t,h), axis=-1)
    er = np.stack((np.cos(psi), np.sin(psi), np.zeros_like(psi)), axis=-1)
    et = np.stack((-np.sin(psi), np.cos(psi), np.zeros_like(psi)), axis=-1)
    ez = np.zeros_like(er)
    ez[:, 2] = 1
    W = np.stack((er,et,ez), axis=-1)
    orientation = W @ np.swapaxes(B, 1, 2)
    center = major*er
    contact = center + radius*np.einsum("nij,nj->ni", orientation, g)
    target = (major+radius)*er
    omega = (1-gear)*ez - (gear*kg)[:, None]*er
    analytic_slip = major*et + np.cross(omega, radius*er)
    # Separate finite-difference check of the actual SO(3) path:
    dQ = np.gradient(orientation, psi, axis=0, edge_order=2)
    dC = np.gradient(center, psi, axis=0, edge_order=2)
    spin_matrix = dQ @ np.swapaxes(orientation, 1, 2)
    omega_fd = np.stack((spin_matrix[:,2,1], spin_matrix[:,0,2],
                         spin_matrix[:,1,0]), axis=-1)
    slip_fd = dC + np.cross(omega_fd, radius*er)
    actual_laps = gear*2*np.pi/length
    summary = {
        "cam_amplitude": float(amplitude),
        "cam_length": length,
        "sphere_and_tube_radius": float(radius),
        "torus_major": float(major),
        "reduced_radius_gear": float(gear),
        "actual_cam_cycles": float(actual_laps),
        "historical_even_winding_satisfied": bool(abs(actual_laps-even_cycles)<1e-8),
        "normal_spin_min": float((-gear*kg).min()),
        "normal_spin_max": float((-gear*kg).max()),
        "wall_position_max_residual": float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(contact-target,axis=-1))),
        "torus_implicit_max_residual": float(np.max(np.abs((np.hypot(contact[:,0],contact[:,1])-major)**2+contact[:,2]**2-radius**2))),
        "orientation_orthogonality_max_residual": float(np.max(np.abs(np.swapaxes(orientation,1,2)@orientation-np.eye(3)))),
        "orientation_seam_frobenius": float(np.linalg.norm(orientation[0]-orientation[-1])),
        "analytical_contact_slip_max": float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(analytic_slip,axis=-1))),
        "finite_difference_slip_max_interior": float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(slip_fd[10:-10],axis=-1))),
    }
    return summary, orientation


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    p.add_argument("--amplitude", type=float, default=0.22)
    p.add_argument("--radius", type=float, default=.55)
    p.add_argument("--cycles", type=int, default=4)
    p.add_argument("--major", type=float)
    p.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=2400)
    p.add_argument("--check", action="store_true")
    args = p.parse_args()
    report, _ = solve_cam(args.amplitude, args.radius, args.cycles, args.steps, args.major)
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))
    if args.check:
        if report["wall_position_max_residual"] > 1e-10 or report["analytical_contact_slip_max"] > 1e-10:
            raise SystemExit("FAIL: selected-contact constraint")
        if args.major is None and (not report["historical_even_winding_satisfied"] or report["orientation_seam_frobenius"] > 1e-8):
            raise SystemExit("FAIL: intended closed cam return")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
'''

"""Sandboxed GrAnn material-cam rolling reconstruction.

This is a nominated-contact SO(3) mechanism, not the historical self-crossing
Great Annulum or a globally no-slip b=a torus-sphere contact.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import cumulative_trapezoid
from scipy.interpolate import PchipInterpolator


def latitude_cam(theta, amplitude):
    """Unit-sphere material path with closed nonzero geodesic curvature."""
    theta = np.asarray(theta, dtype=float)
    beta = amplitude * np.sin(2 * theta)
    db = 2 * amplitude * np.cos(2 * theta)
    ddb = -4 * amplitude * np.sin(2 * theta)
    er = np.stack((np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta), np.zeros_like(theta)), axis=-1)
    et = np.stack((-np.sin(theta), np.cos(theta), np.zeros_like(theta)), axis=-1)
    ez = np.array([0., 0., 1.])
    g = np.cos(beta)[..., None] * er + np.sin(beta)[..., None] * ez
    gp = (-db * np.sin(beta))[..., None] * er + np.cos(beta)[..., None] * et + (db * np.cos(beta))[..., None] * ez
    gpp = (-(ddb * np.sin(beta) + db**2 * np.cos(beta) + np.cos(beta)))[..., None] * er - (2 * db * np.sin(beta))[..., None] * et + (ddb * np.cos(beta) - db**2 * np.sin(beta))[..., None] * ez
    speed = np.linalg.norm(gp, axis=-1)
    tangent = gp / speed[..., None]
    h = np.cross(g, tangent)
    kg = np.sum(g * np.cross(gp, gpp), axis=-1) / speed**3
    return g, tangent, h, speed, kg


def solve_cam(amplitude=0.22, radius=0.55, even_cycles=4, steps=2400,
              major=None, grid=25001):
    if radius <= 0 or even_cycles < 2 or even_cycles % 2:
        raise ValueError("Need positive radius and positive even GrAnn cycles")
    th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, grid)
    speed = latitude_cam(th, amplitude)[3]
    arc = cumulative_trapezoid(speed, th, initial=0)
    length = float(arc[-1])
    if major is None:
        major = radius * (even_cycles*length/(2*np.pi) - 1)
    if major <= radius:
        raise ValueError("Selected major radius does not give a ring torus")
    gear = (major+radius)/radius
    psi = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, steps+1)
    s = gear*psi
    lap = np.floor(s/length + 1e-12)
    remainder = np.clip(s-lap*length, 0, length)
    theta = PchipInterpolator(arc, th)(remainder) + 2*np.pi*lap
    g,t,h,_,kg = latitude_cam(theta, amplitude)
    B = np.stack((g,t,h), axis=-1)
    er = np.stack((np.cos(psi), np.sin(psi), np.zeros_like(psi)), axis=-1)
    et = np.stack((-np.sin(psi), np.cos(psi), np.zeros_like(psi)), axis=-1)
    ez = np.zeros_like(er)
    ez[:, 2] = 1
    W = np.stack((er,et,ez), axis=-1)
    orientation = W @ np.swapaxes(B, 1, 2)
    center = major*er
    contact = center + radius*np.einsum("nij,nj->ni", orientation, g)
    target = (major+radius)*er
    omega = (1-gear)*ez - (gear*kg)[:, None]*er
    analytic_slip = major*et + np.cross(omega, radius*er)
    # Separate finite-difference check of the actual SO(3) path:
    dQ = np.gradient(orientation, psi, axis=0, edge_order=2)
    dC = np.gradient(center, psi, axis=0, edge_order=2)
    spin_matrix = dQ @ np.swapaxes(orientation, 1, 2)
    omega_fd = np.stack((spin_matrix[:,2,1], spin_matrix[:,0,2],
                         spin_matrix[:,1,0]), axis=-1)
    slip_fd = dC + np.cross(omega_fd, radius*er)
    actual_laps = gear*2*np.pi/length
    summary = {
        "cam_amplitude": float(amplitude),
        "cam_length": length,
        "sphere_and_tube_radius": float(radius),
        "torus_major": float(major),
        "reduced_radius_gear": float(gear),
        "actual_cam_cycles": float(actual_laps),
        "historical_even_winding_satisfied": bool(abs(actual_laps-even_cycles)<1e-8),
        "normal_spin_min": float((-gear*kg).min()),
        "normal_spin_max": float((-gear*kg).max()),
        "wall_position_max_residual": float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(contact-target,axis=-1))),
        "torus_implicit_max_residual": float(np.max(np.abs((np.hypot(contact[:,0],contact[:,1])-major)**2+contact[:,2]**2-radius**2))),
        "orientation_orthogonality_max_residual": float(np.max(np.abs(np.swapaxes(orientation,1,2)@orientation-np.eye(3)))),
        "orientation_seam_frobenius": float(np.linalg.norm(orientation[0]-orientation[-1])),
        "analytical_contact_slip_max": float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(analytic_slip,axis=-1))),
        "finite_difference_slip_max_interior": float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(slip_fd[10:-10],axis=-1))),
    }
    return summary, orientation


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    p.add_argument("--amplitude", type=float, default=0.22)
    p.add_argument("--radius", type=float, default=.55)
    p.add_argument("--cycles", type=int, default=4)
    p.add_argument("--major", type=float)
    p.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=2400)
    p.add_argument("--check", action="store_true")
    args = p.parse_args()
    report, _ = solve_cam(args.amplitude, args.radius, args.cycles, args.steps, args.major)
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))
    if args.check:
        if report["wall_position_max_residual"] > 1e-10 or report["analytical_contact_slip_max"] > 1e-10:
            raise SystemExit("FAIL: selected-contact constraint")
        if args.major is None and (not report["historical_even_winding_satisfied"] or report["orientation_seam_frobenius"] > 1e-8):
            raise SystemExit("FAIL: intended closed cam return")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    dg/ds=t;
    dt/ds=-g+kappa_g h;
    dh/ds=-kappa_g t.

    omega=(psi_dot-s_dot)e_z - kappa_g(s)*s_dot*e_r.

    dC = np.gradient(center, psi, axis=0, edge_order=2)
    spin_matrix = dQ @ np.swapaxes(orientation, 1, 2)
    omega_fd = np.stack((spin_matrix[:,2,1], spin_matrix[:,0,2],
                         spin_matrix[:,1,0]), axis=-1)
    slip_fd = dC + np.cross(omega_fd, radius*er)
    actual_laps = gear*2*np.pi/length
    summary = {
        "cam_amplitude": float(amplitude),
        "cam_length": length,
        "sphere_and_tube_radius": float(radius),
        "torus_major": float(major),
        "reduced_radius_gear": float(gear),
        "actual_cam_cycles": float(actual_laps),
        "historical_even_winding_satisfied": bool(abs(actual_laps-even_cycles)<1e-8),
        "normal_spin_min": float((-gear*kg).min()),
        "normal_spin_max": float((-gear*kg).max()),
        "wall_position_max_residual": float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(contact-target,axis=-1))),
        "torus_implicit_max_residual": float(np.max(np.abs((np.hypot(contact[:,0],contact[:,1])-major)**2+contact[:,2]**2-radius**2))),
        "orientation_orthogonality_max_residual": float(np.max(np.abs(np.swapaxes(orientation,1,2)@orientation-np.eye(3)))),
        "orientation_seam_frobenius": float(np.linalg.norm(orientation[0]-orientation[-1])),
        "analytical_contact_slip_max": float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(analytic_slip,axis=-1))),
        "finite_difference_slip_max_interior": float(np.max(np.linalg.norm(slip_fd[10:-10],axis=-1))),
    }
    return summary, orientation


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    p.add_argument("--amplitude", type=float, default=0.22)
    p.add_argument("--radius", type=float, default=.55)
    p.add_argument("--cycles", type=int, default=4)
    p.add_argument("--major", type=float)
    p.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=2400)
    p.add_argument("--check", action="store_true")
    args = p.parse_args()
    report, _ = solve_cam(args.amplitude, args.radius, args.cycles, args.steps, args.major)
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))
    if args.check:
        if report["wall_position_max_residual"] > 1e-10 or report["analytical_contact_slip_max"] > 1e-10:
            raise SystemExit("FAIL: selected-contact constraint")
        if args.major is None and (not report["historical_even_winding_satisfied"] or report["orientation_seam_frobenius"] > 1e-8):
            raise SystemExit("FAIL: intended closed cam return")

    main()

## The likely purpose of GrAnn

I think we've found the missing function: **GrAnn is a mechanical connection that converts the geometry of a curve into rotational transport.** It is not simply a gear, a track, or an additional projection surface.

More specifically, it appears intended to do three jobs:

1. **Couple translation to rotation.** The sphere's passage around the torus determines how far its material contact advances along GrAnn.
2. **Transmit curvature into orientation.** GrAnn's changing tangent and curvature determine how the sphere twists during that motion, which can change how the R/Q crossbar and gimbal elbow move.
3. **Enforce a shared return.** The apparatus must reconcile the torus orbit, GrAnn's winding, and the resulting orientation, rather than allowing each to acquire an arbitrary phase.

That interpretation is consistent with the historical goal: the Whirligig is meant to find a geometrical relationship between two equations by tracing the motion *forced by their coupling*, not by combining their outputs through an independently invented formula.

And there is a more interesting mathematical reason to think this is correct.

## The missing degree of freedom

Take the sphere of radius \(b\) rolling along the torus, with its center following \(C(\psi)=R\mathbf e_r(\psi)\).

At the chosen wall contact, rolling without slip requires

\[
\dot C+\boldsymbol\omega\times(b\mathbf e_r)=0.
\]

But this condition does **not** determine the sphere's complete angular velocity. Rotation about the contact normal \(\mathbf e_r\) remains free.

That's the missing channel GrAnn can constrain.

Instead of prescribing an extra rotation, give the sphere a material track \(G(s)\), parameterized by its own spherical arc length. Define its tangent and surface-normal frame:

\[
\mathbf t=\frac{dG}{ds},
\qquad
\mathbf h=G\times\mathbf t.
\]

Match that moving frame to the torus's radial, tangential, and vertical frame. The resulting orientation is

\[
\boxed{
Q(\psi)=
[\mathbf e_r,\mathbf e_\varphi,\mathbf e_z]\,
[G,\mathbf t,\mathbf h]^{T}
}
\]

Now the rolling constraint determines how fast the contact advances around GrAnn:

\[
\boxed{\frac{ds}{d\psi}=\frac{R+b}{b}}
\]

And the complete angular velocity becomes

\[
\boxed{
\boldsymbol\omega=
(\dot\psi-\dot s)\mathbf e_z
-\kappa_g(s)\dot s\,\mathbf e_r
}
\]

where \(\kappa_g\) is GrAnn's **geodesic curvature** on the sphere.

The second term is the important discovery. The curvature of GrAnn determines the rotational degree of freedom that ordinary point-contact rolling leaves undetermined.

A great circle has \(\kappa_g=0\), so the current approximation suppresses precisely that additional curvature-to-rotation coupling.

## A working proof of concept

I tested this with a family of closed curves on the sphere:

\[
G_A(\theta)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos\beta\cos\theta\\
\cos\beta\sin\theta\\
\sin\beta
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\beta=A\sin(2\theta).
\]

Here \(A=0\) gives the great-circle control. Nonzero \(A\) gives a curved material track that induces additional sphere rotation.

The results:

| Property | Great circle | Curved GrAnn candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| Track amplitude | 0 | 0.22 |
| Track length | 6.2832 | 6.5030 |
| Torus major radius for four GrAnn circuits | 1.6500 | 1.7270 |
| Additional contact-normal spin | Zero | Up to ±2.899 per orbital radian |
| Selected-contact slip residual | ~3 × 10⁻¹⁶ | ~3 × 10⁻¹⁶ |
| Full orientation closes | Yes | Yes |

After aligning their starting orientations, the curved track makes the sphere's orientation differ from the great-circle control by as much as **0.829 radians during the orbit**, before returning to the starting orientation.

This is genuine kinematic coupling in the proposed model. We are getting an additional rotation from the contact curve's geometry, rather than adding an arbitrary oscillator.

### GrAnn also determines the permitted gearing

If the complete GrAnn track has spherical arc length \(L_G\), the number of GrAnn circuits per torus orbit becomes

\[
\boxed{
m_G=\frac{2\pi(R+b)}{bL_G}
}
\]

For the historical even-winding condition, \(m_G\) must be an even integer.

This is a substantial correction. Our previous 4:1 gearing assumed GrAnn's length was \(2\pi\). With the curved experimental track, keeping the old radius produces only **3.8648 GrAnn circuits** and fails orientation closure.

So GrAnn helps determine which geometric configurations are actually admissible.

## How I would reconstruct the complete instrument

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box align="center" gap={1}>
    **GrAnn material track**
    <caption>Arc length, tangent, geodesic curvature, and return phase</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Torus-contact constraint**
    <caption>Determines full sphere orientation and curvature-induced spin</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Transported R/Q sweep planes**
    <caption>Intersect both independent curves and solve for their moving contacts</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Crossbar and one perpendicular gimbal elbow**
    <caption>Transport input tangent and curvature information without an extra projector</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center"><icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/></row>
  <box align="center" gap={1}>
    **Curvy Lisa**
    <caption>The mechanically determined torus-wall trace, to be tested as a candidate relational operator</caption>
  </box>
</box>

Notice the change: rather than calculating the two curve positions and spinning the sphere around them, **the GrAnn contact frame determines the moving geometry in which the two curves are interrogated**.

That is how its curvature reaches the crossbar and elbow.

### What about the strange self-intersection?

I suspect the `GrAnn_Omph` intersection and antipodal tangency are intended to provide **branch switching and holonomy comparison**: the mechanism can revisit a geometric anchor after different paths, preserving information about the rotations accumulated along each.

But that's still a hypothesis. The curvature-to-spin function works without a self-intersection. We should compare a great circle, a simply curved loop, and a properly anchored self-intersecting track to discover whether that topology supplies additional mathematical functionality.

There's also a correction to our previous diagnostics: the historical \(i_r\) is a distinguished R-side anchor. GrAnn need not pass through **every moving R follower point**. Our earlier maximum-gap test was therefore not a valid test of the `GrAnn_Omph` anchor condition.

## Saved to HsH

I committed both the mathematical reconstruction and a runnable numerical experiment:

<box gap={2}>
  <row align="start" gap={2}>
    <icon name="file-text" color="secondary"/>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **[GrAnn functional reconstruction](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/tools/whirligig_rq/GRANN_FUNCTIONAL_RECONSTRUCTION_2026-10-18.md)**
      <caption>Derivation, numerical results, original constraints, negative controls, and proposed R/Q integration</caption>
    </box>
  </row>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <row align="start" gap={2}>
    <icon name="file-code" color="secondary"/>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **[Runnable GrAnn curvature/rolling prototype](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/tools/whirligig_rq/grann_darboux_experiment.py)**
      <caption>Python/NumPy/SciPy simulation with contact, rotation, slip, and winding diagnostics</caption>
      <text size="xs"><Link url="sandbox:/mnt/data/grann_darboux_experiment.py" title="Local prototype file"/></text>
    </box>
  </row>
</box>

The code ran successfully with the curved-track, great-circle, and nonclosing negative-control configurations. I have not yet substituted it into the website, because the transported R/Q sweep and single-elbow constraints must be integrated and tested together.

**My working conclusion:** GrAnn's essential function is to convert the geometric curvature of a material track into constrained rotational motion, then transmit that motion into the two-equation comparison. The distinctive GrAnn topology may add a second function involving branch transitions and holonomy, but we can now investigate that separately instead of guessing a shape.

And the final scientific gate remains: even a successfully coupled Curvy Lisa is not automatically a derivative \(dQ/dR\). We will have to demonstrate which relationship the resulting operator actually preserves.

[L2]   "content": "#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Sandboxed GrAnn material-cam rolling reconstruction.

This is a nominated-contact SO(3) mechanism, not the historical self-crossing
Great Annulum or a globally no-slip b=a torus-sphere contact.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import cumulative_trapezoid
from scipy.interpolate import PchipInterpolator


def latitude_cam(theta, amplitude):
    """Unit-sphere material path with closed nonzero geodesic curvature."""
    theta = np.asarray(theta, dtype=float)
    beta = amplitude * np.sin(2 * theta)
    db = 2 * amplitude * np.cos(2 * theta)
    ddb = -4 * amplitude * np.sin(2 * theta)
    er = np.stack((np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta), np.zeros_like(theta)), axis=-1)
    et = np.stack((-np.sin(theta), np.cos(theta), np.zeros_like(theta)), axis=-1)
    ez = np.array([0., 0., 1.])
    g = np.cos(beta)[..., None] * er + np.sin(beta)[..., None] * ez
    gp = (-db * np.sin(beta))[..., None] * er + np.cos(beta)[..., None] * et + (db * np.cos(beta))[..., None] * ez
    gpp = (-(ddb * np.sin(beta) + db**2 * np.cos(beta) + np.cos(beta)))[..., None] * er - (2 * db * np.sin(beta))[..., None] * et + (ddb * np.cos(beta) - db**2 * np.sin(beta))[..., None] * ez
    speed = np.linalg.norm(gp, axis=-1)
    tangent = gp / speed[..., None]
    h = np.cross(g, tangent)
    kg = np.sum(g * np.cross(gp, gpp), axis=-1) / speed**3
    return g, tangent, h, speed, kg


def solve_cam(amplitude=0.22, radius=0.55, even_cycles=4, steps=2400,
              major=None, grid=25001):
    if radius <= 0 or even_cycles < 2 or even_cycles % 2:
        raise ValueError("Need positive radius and positive even GrAnn cycles")
    th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, grid)
    speed = latitude_cam(th, amplitude)[3]
    arc = cumulative_trapezoid(speed, th, initial=0)
    length = float(arc[-1])
    if major is None:
        major = radius * (even_cycles*length/(2*np.pi) - 1)
    if major <= radius:
        raise ValueError("Selected major radius does not give a ring torus")
    gear = (major+radius)/radius
    psi = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, steps+1)
    s = gear*psi
    lap = np.floor(s/length + 1e-12)
    remainder = np.clip(s-lap*length, 0, length)
    theta = PchipInterpolator(arc, th)(remainder) + 2*np.pi*lap
    g,t,h,_,kg = latitude_cam(theta, amplitude)
    B = np.stack((g,t,h), axis=-1)
    er = np.stack((np.cos(psi), np.sin(psi), np.zeros_like(psi)), axis=-1)
    et = np.stack((-np.sin(psi), np.cos(psi), np.zeros_like(psi)), axis=-1)
    ez = np.zeros_like(er)
    ez[:, 2] = 1
    W = np.stack((er,et,ez), axis=-1)
    orientation = W @ np.swapaxes(B, 1, 2)
    center = major*er
    contact = center + radius*np.einsum("nij,nj->ni", orientation, g)

Two input curves R and Q must generate a RELATIONAL output, not a decorative direct superposition. GrAnn is constrained at the outer torus wall, with a special anchor at i_r, an antipodal tangency and an even material-circuit return. The independently sliding R/Q contacts define a varying bar, W_obble and its normal plane W_iggle, whose ONE elbow/ray writes Curvy Lisa on the torus. The archival output Q-with-respect-to-R was called a derivative, but no derivative operator was formally specified.

Let torus major radius R0, equal torus tube and sphere radius b=a, and torus orbital angle psi. Fix a selected outer-wall point P=(R0+b)e_r and C=R0 e_r. Rolling at that point demands:

    C_dot + omega cross (b e_r) = 0.

The equation cannot constrain spin around the contact normal e_r because e_r cross e_r=0. Thus a rolling ratio alone does NOT determine the sphere's full orientation.

**Functional interpretation:** GrAnn should be a material cam/contact curve G(s) on the sphere which determines this missing spin via its geodesic curvature, and transfers a path-dependent frame into the R/Q intersection selector and the gimbal elbow.

Take G(s)=g(s) as a unit-sphere curve parameterized by ACTUAL spherical arc length s. Set t=dg/ds, h=g cross t, signed kappa_g=(dt/ds).h, B(s)=[g,t,h], W(psi)=[e_r,e_phi,e_z], and Q=W B^T.

Modeling intervention: align the material contact tangent with the torus track tangent so Qg=e_r, Qt=e_phi and Qh=e_z. This is the simplest candidate for the historical, underdetermined cam-bearing contact rule.

The spherical Darboux frame obeys:

    dg/ds=t;
    dt/ds=-g+kappa_g h;
    dh/ds=-kappa_g t.

This gives the sphere's exact world angular velocity:

    omega=(psi_dot-s_dot)e_z - kappa_g(s)*s_dot*e_r.

Substituting into the nominated no-slip constraint yields:

    ds/dpsi = (R0+b)/b.

Thus the missing component is NOT an arbitrary dial:

    omega.e_r = -kappa_g(s)*s_dot.

The **geodesic curvature of GrAnn determines the contact-normal spin**. For a great-circle surrogate, kappa_g=0, so this channel is erased. Let L_G be the actual length of one GrAnn material cycle on the UNIT sphere. In one torus orbit the cam advances by 2*pi*(R0+b)/b of dimensionless spherical arc length. The number of completed GrAnn circuits is therefore

The historical even-multiple condition m_G=2k fixes a resonance:

## 🌀 Whirligig status, October 18

**We've identified a plausible missing mechanical function for GrAnn and built a working numerical prototype. The next job is integrating that mechanism into the complete R/Q apparatus.**

<box gap={2}>
  <row align="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="check-circle" color="success"/>
    **GrAnn curvature-to-rotation mechanism derived and tested**
  </row>
  <row align="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="check-circle" color="success"/>
    **Prototype and research notes committed to HsH**
  </row>
  <row align="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="clock" color="secondary"/>
    **GrAnn-to-R/Q crossbar and elbow integration pending**
  </row>
  <row align="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="clock" color="secondary"/>
    **Historical GrAnn self-intersection and tangency unresolved**
  </row>
</box>

### What we've established

The proposed mechanism uses GrAnn's curvature to determine a component of sphere rotation that the ordinary rolling-contact condition leaves free.

\[
\boxed{\omega_{\mathrm{normal}}=-\kappa_g(s)\dot{s}}
\]

That gives us a **mechanical route from the shape of GrAnn to the orientation of the sphere**, without inventing an independent spin control.

I just reran the committed Python prototype, including the great-circle control and a deliberately nonclosing case.

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Curved GrAnn, four circuits | Passes contact and closure tests |
| Great-circle control | Zero extra contact-normal spin |
| Curved GrAnn with old fixed radius | Fails full-orientation closure |
| Maximum analytical contact-slip residual, curved example | \(3.3\times10^{-16}\) |
| Curved example's orientation seam residual | \(1.2\times10^{-15}\) |

These are checks of the proposed selected-point contact mechanism, not yet tests of the full Whirligig.

### The remaining engineering work

The critical chain still needs to be connected:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2} align="center">
  **GrAnn material track**
  <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  **Torus-constrained sphere rotation**
  <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  **Transported R/Q sweep plane**
  <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  **Sliding crossbar and perpendicular elbow**
  <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary"/>
  **Curvy Lisa on the torus wall**
</box>

The current website source still uses the **older great-circle GrAnn approximation**. It does not yet use the newly derived curvature-to-spin mechanism to control the R/Q contacts or elbow. I also attempted to access the live Whirligig page, but it was inaccessible from my browser tool, so the deployed version remains unverified.

### What I recommend next

We should implement the GrAnn material-track engine inside the R/Q solver, then compare three constructions under identical inputs: the great-circle control, a smoothly curved GrAnn, and eventually a self-intersecting GrAnn.

That will tell us whether the historical self-intersection actually contributes essential branch or holonomy information, rather than assuming it must.

The work is preserved here:

- <Link url="https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/tools/whirligig_rq/GRANN_FUNCTIONAL_RECONSTRUCTION_2026-10-18.md" title="GrAnn mathematical reconstruction"/>
- <Link url="https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/tools/whirligig_rq/grann_darboux_experiment.py" title="Runnable numerical prototype"/>

**Bottom line:** We've moved from reproducing the described apparatus to testing what mechanical purpose it could serve. The curvature-to-spin mechanism is a promising, mathematically concrete result. Now it has to demonstrate that it changes the *relational output of R and Q* in a useful, reproducible way. That's our next decisive test.

thoughts.content: I’m interpreting this as a correction: GrAnn should enforce minimal geometric closure, cycle the sphere through all three axes, and synchronize elbow rotations to a common denominator—not merely lock curvature spin.

I’m treating GrAnn-R/Q as a synchronization layer, not a curvature-driven force. I’ll define closure as the smallest shared rotational period across all three sphere axes and elbow phases, then verify the interpretation against the existing design.

[L2]   "content": "# GrAnn → Torus Wall | Selected-contact mechanical reconstruction

**Status:** SANDBOXED mechanical carrier implemented; FULL HISTORICAL GRANN NOT RECONSTRUCTED  
**Date:** 2026-10-18  
**Browser source:** `PUBLIC_SITE/instruments/whirligig/index.html`  
**Reconstruction commits:** `215f83ff9775021cd321fdcd73d5dbf7cb925f70` (constraint), `8c0aa800e7b6697e5144fdeacf70ac87ec8af36d` (drawing)  
**Reference engine:** `tools/whirligig_rq/whirligig.py`, particularly `frame_and_roll`.

## Nathan Direct source constraints

The original 3D toy is transcribed in [FINDING THE DONUT, pp. 25–27](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/_AUTO_EXTRACTED_TEXT/FINDING%20THE%20DONUT%20(nolat).txt).

The construction specifies: GrAnn self-intersection `GrAnn_Omph` at the R-side point `i_r`; the antipodal `GrAnn_t_ipode` self-tangent; `P_ivot` simultaneously on GrAnn and `TorOuRad`; `Donomphulon` moving along `TorInCirc`; `BigRad` through the Donut center, Donomphulon and P_ivot; sphere rolling with **even multiple of GrAnn circuits per outer-torus circuit**; and Curvy Lisa written by the single constrained perpendicular elbow on the torus. The original text calls this the **3D toy version**.

**Source limitation:** The historical excerpt specifies the two special self-intersection/tangency constraints but does not provide a unique analytic parameterization of a self-intersecting Great Annulum. A great circle is therefore a partial carrier model, not the full named GrAnn. Do not invent that missing topology or claim `GrAnn_Omph=i_r` is satisfied.

## Implemented contact-driven kinematics

Let `R` be the torus major radius; `a=b` the torus tube radius and sphere radius. Let `ψ` denote the torus-centerline orbital angle. The chosen GrAnn contact-phase speed is

```text
gear = (R+a)/b    (historical even winding requires gear=2n, n positive integer)
γ(ψ) = gear · ψ
r_GrAnn_body(ψ) = (sin γ, 0, cos γ)
W(ψ) = (e_r, e_phi, e_z)
B(γ) = (r_GrAnn, t_GrAnn, n_GrAnn)
Q(ψ) = W(ψ) · B(γ)^T
P_ivot(ψ) = (R+a) e_r(ψ)             // constrained outer wall
C(ψ) = P_ivot(ψ) − b Q(ψ)r_GrAnn(ψ) // center DERIVED from wall contact
GrAnn_carrier(λ;ψ) = C(ψ)+b Q(ψ)(sin λ,0,cos λ)
Donomphulon(ψ) = (R−a) e_r(ψ)       // inner torus circumference
GrAnn_antipode = C(ψ) − b Q(ψ)r_GrAnn(ψ)
BigRad: origin ↔ P_ivot, containing Donomphulon.
```

The browser derives C from the outer-wall pivot and GrAnn body contact rather than positioning C independently and merely drawing a ring afterward. This is an explicit selected-contact kinematic constraint, although **for this particular orientation it algebraically reproduces the earlier center path**. It does *not yet* add the full source-described force/kinematic influence of an intersecting GrAnn on the R follower and composite elbow. Do not represent that incomplete part as solved.

At `a=b`, the opposite point of the selected great-circle carrier is at the inner torus circumference. That is a consequence of this degenerate equal-radius contact construction, not a proof of no-slip across the entire contact circle.

Selected-contact rolling condition per unit `ψ`:
```text
dC/dψ + ω × (b e_r) = 0;   ω=(0,0,−R/b).
```
The simultaneous GrAnn/contact conditions depend on `ψ`; the independent R/Q sweep-plane contact selection and single perpendicular elbow remain unchanged from the prior browser instrument.

## Browser diagnostics

The revised UI includes a panel named **GrAnn torus-wall coupling**, plus a 4:1 historical even-winding reference button. The sphere body-frame view shows the magenta great-circle carrier with its gold moving selected contact and blue antipode. The world/toroidal view shows the carrier, gold `P_ivot`, blue `Donomphulon`, and `BigRad`. The panel numerically reports:
- `P_ivot` deviation from outer torus implicit surface and the contact constraint;
- antipode-to-Donomphulon coincidence and inner torus wall residual;
- BigRad collinearity;
- selected-point rolling velocity residual;
- gear ratio and whether **an even integer per individual torus orbit** is satisfied;
- **R-side input anchor distance from the great-circle proxy**, specifically exposing the unimplemented `GrAnn_Omph` coincidence.

The UI permits non-even radius settings for exploration but marks them **NOT EVEN**, rather than silently certifying full historical compliance. The default `R=1.65, a=b=0.55` yields gear `4`, an even integer.

## Executed numerical tests

JS syntax validated; a stub DOM/canvas executed 31 scenarios: default, each of 14 equation profiles on R, each of 14 on Q, a non-even gear negative control, and restoration to 4:1 gearing. All 1,651 samples in each configuration had first-forward elbow-to-torus intersections, zero east/west hemisphere violations, and normalized crossbar/elbow orthogonality errors no more than `4.7×10⁻¹⁶`. Maximum numerical wall-pivot, inner wall, inner antipode, BigRad alignment and selected-contact velocity errors across these tests were each below `10⁻¹⁵`. The non-even test (`R=1.60, a=b=.55`, ratio `43/11`) was correctly marked noncompliant; the even reference button restored 4:1. Canvas rendering callbacks executed.

**Critical unmet original constraint:** In the default configuration the *maximum gap* between the source R-side moving point and this carrier's plane is about **0.302 in the model's distance units** (not zero). This quantifies why the great-circle carrier is not yet the required self-intersecting GrAnn with Omph fixed at `i_r`. The full GrAnn topology and its influence on the equation follower must be recovered or independently derived, then tested, before claiming complete coupled apparatus reconstruction.

No live browser smoke test or ChatGPT Sites deployment was performed. A GitHub file update is not a Sites publication.

## Next derivation target

Recover or specify an explicit curve `G(u;ψ)` on the sphere satisfying simultaneously:

1. Self-intersection at `i_r(ψ)` (two parameters with same 3D point but independent directions);
2. Opposite special tangency at `t_ipode`, with intended parameter/normal convention clarified;
3. `P_ivot∈G` AND `P_ivot∈TorOuRad`;
4. A moving `Donomphulon∈TorInCirc` and the requested BigRad alignment;
5. Rolling orientation plus even GrAnn winding per torus orbit;
6. Coupled influence on actual crossbar/elbow motion, with no extra projector.

A parameterization cannot be declared solved by replacing GrAnn with an unconstrained great circle or a free oscillator. Record failures and incompatible constraints explicitly.

[L1] {
[L2]   "content": "# GrAnn as a curvature-to-spin connection: functional reconstruction

**Status:** SANDBOXED derivation and executed NumPy/SciPy numerical tests, not a full reconstruction of historical GrAnn, and not published to the live website. **Date:** 2026-10-18.

Sources: Nathan's FINDING THE DONUT pp. 23–27; the R/Q Whirligig Python solver and README; the 2026-10-09 Whirligig continuity handoff. The mechanism proposed below is a new inference from those source constraints, not a claim that its equations were explicitly specified in the source.

## Historical functional target

Two input curves R and Q must generate a RELATIONAL output, not a decorative direct superposition. GrAnn is constrained at the outer torus wall, with a special anchor at i_r, an antipodal tangency and an even material-circuit return. The independently sliding R/Q contacts define a varying bar, W_obble and its normal plane W_iggle, whose ONE elbow/ray writes Curvy Lisa on the torus. The archival output Q-with-respect-to-R was called a derivative, but no derivative operator was formally specified.

## Recovered missing degree of freedom

Let torus major radius R0, equal torus tube and sphere radius b=a, and torus orbital angle psi. Fix a selected outer-wall point P=(R0+b)e_r and C=R0 e_r. Rolling at that point demands:

    C_dot + omega cross (b e_r) = 0.

The equation cannot constrain spin around the contact normal e_r because e_r cross e_r=0. Thus a rolling ratio alone does NOT determine the sphere's full orientation.

**Functional interpretation:** GrAnn should be a material cam/contact curve G(s) on the sphere which determines this missing spin via its geodesic curvature, and transfers a path-dependent frame into the R/Q intersection selector and the gimbal elbow.

Take G(s)=g(s) as a unit-sphere curve parameterized by ACTUAL spherical arc length s. Set t=dg/ds, h=g cross t, signed kappa_g=(dt/ds).h, B(s)=[g,t,h], W(psi)=[e_r,e_phi,e_z], and Q=W B^T.

Modeling intervention: align the material contact tangent with the torus track tangent so Qg=e_r, Qt=e_phi and Qh=e_z. This is the simplest candidate for the historical, underdetermined cam-bearing contact rule.

The spherical Darboux frame obeys:

    dg/ds=t;
    dt/ds=-g+kappa_g h;
    dh/ds=-kappa_g t.

This gives the sphere's exact world angular velocity:

    omega=(psi_dot-s_dot)e_z - kappa_g(s)*s_dot*e_r.

Substituting into the nominated no-slip constraint yields:

    ds/dpsi = (R0+b)/b.

import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation
from math import sqrt, pi, lcm

def locked_grann(major=1.65, radius=.55, n=6, samples=1201):
    gear = (major + radius) / radius
    sigma = sqrt(n*n - gear*gear)
    psi = np.linspace(0, 2*pi, samples)
    er = np.column_stack((np.cos(psi), np.sin(psi), np.zeros_like(psi)))
    et = np.column_stack((-np.sin(psi), np.cos(psi), np.zeros_like(psi)))
    # World rotation: orbital Rz followed by a co-rotating GrAnn lock.
    Q = (
        Rotation.from_rotvec(np.column_stack((np.zeros_like(psi), np.zeros_like(psi), psi)))
        * Rotation.from_rotvec(np.outer(psi, np.array([sigma, 0., -gear])))
    ).as_matrix()
    bcontact = np.einsum("nji,nj->ni", Q, er)
    pivot = major*er + radius*np.einsum("nij,nj->ni", Q, bcontact)
    wall = (major+radius)*er
    omega = np.column_stack((sigma*er[:,0], sigma*er[:,1], -major/radius*np.ones_like(psi)))
    slip_analytic = major*et + np.cross(omega, radius*er)
    dQ = np.gradient(Q, psi, axis=0, edge_order=2)
    Omega = dQ@np.swapaxes(Q, 1, 2)
    w_fd = np.column_stack((Omega[:,2,1],Omega[:,0,2],Omega[:,1,0]))
    slip_fd = major*et + np.cross(w_fd, radius*er)
    body_path_length = np.sum(np.linalg.norm(np.diff(bcontact,axis=0), axis=1))
    return dict(gear=gear,grann_turns=n,radial_spin=sigma,axis_omega_ranges={a:(float(omega[:,i].min()),float(omega[:,i].max())) for i,a in enumerate("xyz")},
                max_wall_error=float(np.linalg.norm(pivot-wall,axis=1).max()),
                max_slip=float(np.linalg.norm(slip_analytic,axis=1).max()),
                max_fd_slip=float(np.linalg.norm(slip_fd[5:-5],axis=1).max()),
                orientation_seam=float(np.linalg.norm(Q[0]-Q[-1])),
                measured_material_arclength=float(body_path_length),
                predicted_material_arclength=float(2*pi*gear),
                predicted_single_GrAnn_circuit_length=float(2*pi*gear/n))
for n in (4, 6, 8):
    print(n, locked_grann(n=n) if n>4 else "n=4 is degenerate: no x/y rotation")

That changes the interpretation of GrAnn significantly.

**GrAnn is the rotational synchronizer of the Whirligig.** Its primary job is not to generate extra spin from curvature, as I proposed earlier. It is to impose the smallest shared rotational cycle that closes the complete mechanism.

That means three things:

1. The sphere must complete its required rotations through **all three axes**, not merely spin around its rolling axis.
2. The R and Q curves must return to their starting configurations together, including their orientations and the moving crossbar.
3. The gimbal elbow must be rotationally locked to that common cycle, so its completed revolutions reflect the combined periodicities.

The curvature-to-spin experiment can remain a separate research branch, but it should not determine the main GrAnn locking rule.

## A simpler three-axis GrAnn construction

I tested a candidate that matches your functional description more closely.

Let \(g=(R+b)/b\) be the rolling ratio, and let \(N\) be the smallest admissible shared winding count. Choose the GrAnn radial-spin rate

\[
\sigma=\sqrt{N^2-g^2}.
\]

Then the sphere's angular velocity per unit torus-orbit angle is

\[
\boxed{
\frac{\boldsymbol\omega}{\dot\psi}
=
\sigma\cos\psi\,\hat{\mathbf x}
+\sigma\sin\psi\,\hat{\mathbf y}
-\frac{R}{b}\,\hat{\mathbf z}
}
\]

This uses **all three spatial axes** while preserving the selected-point rolling constraint at the torus wall.

For the existing default \(R=1.65,\ b=0.55\), the old ratio is \(g=4\). Choosing the smallest *even* \(N\) strictly greater than 4 gives **six GrAnn circuits per torus orbit**.

</grid>

In the executed numerical test, X and Y both had nonzero rotational components, Z retained the required rolling component, and the sphere returned to its initial orientation.

This is a candidate **rotational-lock mechanism**, not yet a full R/Q implementation. It avoids requiring GrAnn's shape to generate an arbitrary extra rotation.

### The remaining arithmetic distinction

There are two related quantities we should keep separate:

\[
D=\operatorname{lcm}(q_x,q_y,q_z,q_R,q_Q)
\]

This gives the shortest return duration when the rotational rates are rational fractions \(p_i/q_i\) of a base circuit.

Then the number of completed turns in that duration is \(n_i=Dp_i/q_i\). Their least common multiple can supply the **elbow's gearing count**, if that is the mechanical rule you intend.

Those are not automatically the same number. And although all phases may return arithmetically, we still have to verify that the sphere's full orientation, both curve contacts, and the elbow actually return together.

I've saved the revised design and a separate Python prototype in HsH:

- [GrAnn minimum-return, three-axis locking specification](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/tools/whirligig_rq/GRANN_ROTATIONAL_LOCK_2026-10-18.md)
- [GrAnn rotational-lock prototype](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/tools/whirligig_rq/grann_rotational_lock.py)

The core three-axis construction was numerically tested, and both files were committed and read back. The new standalone CLI has not yet had its own execution check, and **the website has not yet been switched to this mechanism**.

One precise question before I wire the elbow: **When you say “common denominator,” do you want its number of revolutions to be the LCM of the individual completed rotation counts?** For example, if the required counts are 2, 3, and 4, the elbow would make 12 revolutions over their common cycle.
