[Canonical description](../../PUBLIC_SITE/instruments/whirligig/ANALEMMA_CORRECTION_2026-10-21.md). The original GrAnn references below and the older standalone full Python R/Q solver remain research/provenance, **not** implementation equivalence with this latest HTML.

# Whirligig R/Q Engine: rolling sphere, gimbals, two equations, Curvy_Lisa

> **2026-11-02 mechanism distinction:** The current **browser Whirligig** (see `PUBLIC_SITE/instruments/whirligig/index.html`) uses the **INNER torus radial surface** as the selected rolling contact, positive same-direction spin, a minimum even **three-axis Analemma** SO(3) rotational lock, and a single shared sphere-roll / Analemma material phase. The unique gimbal elbow rotates at exactly 2× that phase (four turns per torus orbit), independently of the integer R/Q sweep count. See [the current technical contract](GRANN_INNER_WALL_ROTATIONAL_LOCK_2026-10-21.md). The standalone [grann_rotational_lock.py](grann_rotational_lock.py) has been updated to that branch. **The older full R/Q solver `whirligig.py` described below still uses the separate OUTER-wall selected-contact branch and its own original gimbal/pen implementation. Its results are not proof that the new browser coupling is implemented there.** Do not silently mix the branches or assume that a GitHub update deploys ChatGPT Sites.

**Version:** experimental v0.1, 11 October 2026  
**Status:** SANDBOXED engineering reconstruction. Mathematical/procedural tool, not a proof of a physical isomorphism.

This is a working, configurable **two-equation** mechanism drawn from the historical R/Q / Great Annulum / W_obble / W_iggle / Curvy_Lisa description, together with the archived continuous Navier–Stokes Whirligig Python predecessor. It generates equation curves on a sphere, carries them inside a rolling ball constrained by a torus, uses two genuine orthogonal gimbal hinges to select curve endpoints, constructs the R–Q crossbar and a rotation-minimizing plane perpendicular to it, then intersects a rotating pen ray with the **actual torus quartic** to generate Curvy_Lisa.

**Source provenance:**
- [*FINDING THE DONUT*, pp. 23–27](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/_AUTO_EXTRACTED_TEXT/FINDING%20THE%20DONUT%20(nolat).txt), March 2026.
- [*THE_WHIRLIGIG*](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/HsH-SAT%20Roundup%203/THE_WHIRLIGIG.txt).
- [Existing continuous NS Whirligig source](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS/30SEP26_DUMP/continuous_ns_whirligig_solver%20%281%29.py), independently specifying the sphere's moving contact frame, Bishop connector, torus-wall ray casting, and a Navier–Stokes test setup.
- [*WHIRLIGIG -- REDEFINING SUCCESS*](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/WHIRLIGIG%20--%20REDEFINING%20SUCCESS.txt): a **constructive existence** goal for a back hallway, not a demand for one unique universal derivative.
- Original source distinguishes 3D mechanical toy geometry from actual four-dimensional systems. This code does too.

## Run

```bash
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python whirligig.py --input example_equations.json --out output --search
python plot_mechanics.py --input example_equations.json --out mechanics_snapshot.png --gif rolling_whirligig.gif
python validate_mapping.py --input example_equations.json --out mapping_validation.json
python -m pytest -q
```

`--input` is optional: a two-harmonic-pair demonstration is built in.

## Input equation adapters

Two independent specs are supplied as `R` and `Q` in a JSON file. Every adapter records its representation choice, physical units remain those of the caller, and original numerical coordinates are preserved apart from the sphere carrier. **No universal faithful parameterization exists for arbitrary symbolic equations without specifying a solution branch, observables, and a parameter interval.** Accordingly the tool supports:

| Kind | Example | What is done | Limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| `expression` | `0.5*cos(2*t)+0.1*sin(5*t)` | Scalar function encoded reversibly in sphere latitude; azimuth is `t` | Functions must be finite on the interval. Periodicity tested, not fabricated |
| `parametric` | `{"components":["cos(t)","sin(t)"]}` | 2D trajectory via reversible stereographic embedding; 3D trajectory radialized with magnitude preserved separately | 3D radial projection loses magnitude in its sphere output |
| `implicit` | `x*x/2.25+y*y-1=0` written as `x*x/2.25+y*y-1` | Extract largest closed real zero contour and stereographically lift | Grid approximate; must set bounding box and a suitable branch |
| `ode` | `{"rhs":["y","-x"],"initial":[1,0]}` | Numerically integrates a 1–3 dimensional ODE and embeds the path | May not close; only specified initial-value solution is represented |
| `sampled` | `{"path":"path.csv"}` | Arclength-resamples a closed 2D/3D numeric curve | Intended for PDE/GR/field equations solved upstream; refuses open CSV curves |

Expression parsing is AST-restricted: arithmetic and common NumPy scalar mathematical functions only. No `eval()`, attribute access, user code import, or arbitrary shell expression execution.

For a PDE, differential geometry equation, non-Euclidean metric, or symbolic Schwarzschild geodesic, **first choose a solution and chart** and pass the resulting parametric/CSV path. This prevents smuggling an arbitrary metric into a falsely universal polar-projection routine. Keep the full source equation and domain as metadata outside the low-dimensional carrier.

## Exact selected-contact rolling law

Let the torus have major radius `R` and tube/minor radius `a`. Let the sphere have radius `b<a` and travel on a center circle of radius

\[
\rho=R+a-b,\qquad C(\psi)=\rho(\cos\psi,\sin\psi,0).
\]

The selected contact on the outer equator is

\[
P(\psi)=(R+a)(\cos\psi,\sin\psi,0)=C+b\mathbf e_r.
\]

For rolling without slip at this **isolated chosen point**, the laboratory angular velocity obeys

\[
\boldsymbol\omega=-\frac{\rho}{b}\dot\psi\mathbf e_z,
\quad \dot C+\boldsymbol\omega\times(b\mathbf e_r)=0.
\]

Define the Great-Annulum body contact angle

\[
\gamma(\psi)=\frac{R+a}{b}\psi.
\]

Let `W(ψ)` be the orthonormal world frame `(e_r,e_phi,e_z)` and `B(γ)` the body-frame triad `(r_annulus,t_annulus,n_annulus)`. The **actual orientation** is

\[
\mathcal Q(\psi)=W(\psi)B(\gamma)^T\in SO(3).
\]

`P=C+Q b r_annulus` is tested point by point. A whole-revolution orientation closes when the contact gearing `g=(R+a)/b` is integral. The historical *even multiple* condition is satisfied by choosing `g=6` by default:

- `R=1.6`, `a=0.55`, `b=(R+a)/6=0.358333...`, `rho=1.791666...`.
- A five-point fourth-order finite-difference check of the no-slip velocity converges to zero under grid refinement, while the underlying analytic identity is exact.
- With `b=a` (the originally described limiting sphere size), ball and torus tube share a nonisolated meridional contact set. The program **can render that mode** when `allow_degenerate_contact=true`, but explicitly does **not certify unique-contact rolling**; imposing no slip at every contact point would be overconstrained.

## Gimbal, connector and pen

The input R endpoint is acted on by an internal `Ry(pitch)` hinge; the Q endpoint by an independent `Rx(roll)` hinge. Their axes are perpendicular **by exact construction**. Hinge angles use integer-period rotations with optional sinusoidal modulations. The sphere's physical `SO(3)` rotation is separate from these **internal coordinate controls**. The two endpoints are transported into the lab frame with the exact `Q(ψ)` orientation above.

`W_obble=(R_world+Q_world)/2` is the connector midpoint, and `W_iggle` is the plane perpendicular to the connector. A minimal-rotation Bishop frame supplies its two orthonormal axes. The pen rotates in that plane. Its **first forward** intersection with the torus is found by solving the torus implicit quartic and selecting its smallest positive real root, not by approximating a torus-looking curve.

Optional `align_source_anchors` rotates one source curve **by a single rigid SO(3) alignment**, mapping an off-phase point and tangent on Q to a point and tangent on R. This is a transparent representation intervention, **not an isomorphism proof**, and it is logged with the alignment matrix and both residuals.

An optional Bishop-holonomy correction adjusts the pen's phase around the full circuit. The correction is recorded, and may be disabled: the program does not silently assert that an uncompensated trace must close.

## Results and automatic smoothness search

The `--search` scan varies **four even annulum gear ratios**, pen rotation rates, and independently chosen gimbal rotations. It preserves **all sixty** ranked candidates in `ranked_candidates.json`, including failures; it also saves the selected best candidate's full reproducible arrays, metrics and precision geometry figures. The ranking favors:

- valid mechanical contact, SO(3) orientation and torus quartic intersections;
- nondegenerate sphere/tube clearance;
- both input-equation closures and full orientation closure;
- C¹ seam closure, low curvature variation, low curvature percentile, low high-frequency Fourier tail.

These smoothness thresholds are **engineering filters**, not physical selection laws. C² seam mismatch is reported separately, and smooth candidates must not be mistaken for solutions to the source equations on the other side of their chosen projections. Explicit held-out source-equation residual tests are required before a proposed back hallway is accepted.

For the supplied synthetic two-harmonic pair with independently aligned anchors:

| Diagnostic | Observed |
|---|---:|
| selected contact velocity (analytic) | `0.0` |
| selected contact velocity, 128 samples | `2.14823e-4` |
| selected contact velocity, 256 samples | `1.34990e-5` |
| selected contact velocity, 512 samples | `8.44822e-7` |
| ball-frame closure | `1.73e-15` |
| torus implicit residual | `8.53e-14` |
| Curvy_Lisa positional seam | `8.55e-16` |
| C¹ seam (tangent difference) | `0.00117` |
| R anchor point and tangent gaps | `2.89e-17`, `1.42e-16` |
| response to +1% R amplitude | `0.00287` RMS output shift |
| response to +1% Q amplitude | `0.00903` RMS output shift |

The tests include intentionally nonperiodic inputs and nonintegral rolling gear, both of which must fail the relevant closure checks. Thirteen automated tests passed in the first checked build.

## Files

- `whirligig.py`: generalized two-equation 3D mechanical engine, parsers, closure checks, finite-clearance rolling, search.
- `ui4d.py`: separate, exact six-plane `SO(4)` Universal Indicatrix representation using `y(s)=r(s)R(s)x0`; **not yet coupled to 3D rigid-ball mechanics**.
- `plot_mechanics.py`: precision-drawn sphere/gimbal/annulum/connector/pen figures and optional GIF.
- `validate_mapping.py`: finite-difference grid convergence and independent source-equation perturbations.
- `test_whirligig.py`: 11 regression/negative tests.
- `example_equations.json`: two independent scalar formula inputs with optional anchor alignment.
- `example_ode_vs_implicit.json`: harmonic oscillator versus an ellipse equation.
- `example_historical_limit.json`: equal-radius historical rendering with explicit degeneracy diagnostic.
- `demo/`, `aligned_demo/`: retained 60-run candidate sweeps and selected-best numerical arrays and plots.

## Remaining work

1. **Historic Great Annulum:** source says a self-intersecting annulum with antipodal self-tangent, but does not give its analytic curve. This release makes an explicit great-circle choice. Recover and test the intended self-intersecting annulum before calling this exact historical reconstruction.
2. **4D rolling/gimbal lift:** the sphere/torus apparatus implements the explicitly described **3D toy version**. The separate `ui4d.py` provides its honest SO(4) representation layer, not a fabricated four-dimensional contact geometry.
3. **Joint dynamical derivations:** embedding an equation into a polar curve is not equivalent to deriving an invariant relation from two different equations. Implement input-specific residual or observable maps and compare against held-out predictions in both sectors.
4. **Continuous optimization:** current candidate search is discrete, not a variational or interval-arithmetic global search. Upgrade with constrained smooth optimization, holonomy loops, singularity branch resolution, and complexity/energy budgets.
5. **Metrology and units:** use dimensionless toy geometry until source physical scales and constraints are specified. Do not import GR coefficients into an assumed definition of the engine.

**Research handling:** mathematical apparatus should be assessed independently of speculative framing; no physical claim is inferred from geometric representability alone. Attribution: SAT/H(s)H user and archive research, with original sources linked above; free reuse with citation to source where appropriate.

"""Independent standard-library validation of the Whirligig equal-area Analemma."""
from __future__ import annotations
import math

PI = math.pi
TAU = 2.0 * PI
APERTURE_GAIN = 0.20
ELBOW_ROLL_MULTIPLE = 2


def simpson(f, a: float, b: float, n: int = 8192) -> float:
    if n % 2:
        raise ValueError("Simpson interval count must be even")
    h = (b-a)/n
    total = f(a)+f(b)
    total += 4.0*sum(f(a+(2*i-1)*h) for i in range(1,n//2+1))
    total += 2.0*sum(f(a+2*i*h) for i in range(1,n//2))
    return total*h/3.0


def beta(t: float, k: float) -> float:
    return k*math.sin(t)*math.cos(t)**2


def beta_p(t: float, k: float) -> float:
    s,c=math.sin(t),math.cos(t)
    return k*c*(1.0-3.0*s*s)


def beta_pp(t: float, k: float) -> float:
    s=math.sin(t)
    return k*s*(9.0*s*s-7.0)


def lobe_area(k: float) -> float:
    # d(longitude)/dt=2; north-polar lobe area = integral(1-sin(latitude)) d(longitude).
    return 2.0*simpson(lambda t: 1.0-math.sin(beta(t,k)),0.0,PI)


def speed(t: float, k: float) -> float:
    return math.hypot(beta_p(t,k),2.0*math.cos(beta(t,k)))


def analemma_length(k: float) -> float:
    return simpson(lambda t:speed(t,k),0.0,TAU)


def solve_k() -> float:
    lo,hi=2.5,3.0
    flo=lobe_area(lo)-PI
    fhi=lobe_area(hi)-PI
    if flo*fhi>=0:
        raise RuntimeError("Equal-area root is not bracketed")
    for _ in range(80):
        mid=(lo+hi)/2.0
        fm=lobe_area(mid)-PI
        if flo*fm<=0:
            hi,fhi=mid,fm
        else:
            lo,flo=mid,fm
    return (lo+hi)/2.0


def unit_curve(t: float,k: float):
    be=beta(t,k)
    return (math.cos(be)*math.cos(2*t),math.cos(be)*math.sin(2*t),math.sin(be))


def unit_d1(t: float,k: float):
    be,bp=beta(t,k),beta_p(t,k)
    cb,sb,cp,sp=math.cos(be),math.sin(be),math.cos(2*t),math.sin(2*t)
    return (-bp*sb*cp-2*cb*sp,-bp*sb*sp+2*cb*cp,bp*cb)


def unit_d2(t: float,k: float):
    be,bp,bpp=beta(t,k),beta_p(t,k),beta_pp(t,k)
    cb,sb,cp,sp=math.cos(be),math.sin(be),math.cos(2*t),math.sin(2*t)
    eb=(-sb*cp,-sb*sp,cb)
    ep=(-sp,cp,0.0)
    g=unit_curve(t,k)
    aa=bpp+4*sb*cb
    dd=-4*bp*sb
    qq=-(bp*bp+4*cb*cb)
    return tuple(aa*eb[i]+dd*ep[i]+qq*g[i] for i in range(3))


def dot(a,b):
    return sum(x*y for x,y in zip(a,b))


def cross(a,b):
    return (a[1]*b[2]-a[2]*b[1],a[2]*b[0]-a[0]*b[2],a[0]*b[1])


def norm(a):
    return math.sqrt(dot(a,a))


def main() -> None:
    k=solve_k()
    area_each=lobe_area(k)
    area_both=2*area_each
    area_remainder=4*PI-area_both
    length_unit=analemma_length(k)
    circuits=2
    ratio=1.0+circuits*length_unit/TAU
    delta=ratio-1.0
    sphere_roll_turns_per_orbit=TAU*delta/length_unit
    elbow_turns_per_orbit=ELBOW_ROLL_MULTIPLE*sphere_roll_turns_per_orbit
    b=0.55
    R=ratio*b
    length_physical=length_unit*b
    sphere_circ=TAU*b
    tube_circ=TAU*b
    inner_circ=TAU*(R-b)

    # E: branches at t=0,pi are transverse; W: branches at pi/2,3pi/2 share tangent.
    e1,e2=(2.0,k),(2.0,-k)
    e_det=e1[0]*e2[1]-e1[1]*e2[0]
    w1,w2=(2.0,0.0),(2.0,0.0)
    w_dot=dot(w1,w2)/(norm(w1)*norm(w2))

    # Check analytic derivatives against central differences.
    derivative_errors=[]
    t0=0.713
    for h in (1e-3,5e-4,2.5e-4):
        gm,g0,gp=unit_curve(t0-h,k),unit_curve(t0,k),unit_curve(t0+h,k)
        fd1=tuple((gp[i]-gm[i])/(2*h) for i in range(3))
        fd2=tuple((gp[i]-2*g0[i]+gm[i])/(h*h) for i in range(3))
        derivative_errors.append((h,norm(tuple(fd1[i]-unit_d1(t0,k)[i] for i in range(3))),
                                  norm(tuple(fd2[i]-unit_d2(t0,k)[i] for i in range(3)))))

    min_speed=min(speed(TAU*i/8192,k) for i in range(8192))
    max_lat=2*k/(3*math.sqrt(3))
    midpoint_bound=math.sin(APERTURE_GAIN)

    assert abs(area_each-PI)<2e-11
    assert abs(area_both-area_remainder)<2e-11
    assert abs(e_det)>1e-8
    assert abs(w_dot-1.0)<1e-14
    assert min_speed>1.0
    assert abs(TAU*(ratio-1.0)-circuits*length_unit)<2e-11
    assert abs(sphere_roll_turns_per_orbit-circuits)<2e-12
    assert abs(elbow_turns_per_orbit-ELBOW_ROLL_MULTIPLE*circuits)<2e-12
    assert abs(inner_circ-circuits*length_physical)<2e-11
    assert abs(sphere_circ-tube_circ)<1e-14

    print(f"area-balance shape k                 = {k:.13f}")
    print(f"one lobe area                       = {area_each:.13f} b^2")
    print(f"both lobes area                     = {area_both:.13f} b^2")
    print(f"equatorial remainder area           = {area_remainder:.13f} b^2")
    print(f"maximum lobe latitude               = {math.degrees(max_lat):.9f} deg")
    print(f"full Analemma length / b            = {length_unit:.13f}")
    print(f"minimum even Analemma / sphere-roll circuits = {circuits}")
    print(f"sphere-roll turns per torus orbit    = {sphere_roll_turns_per_orbit:.13f}")
    print(f"elbow multiplier of common roll      = {ELBOW_ROLL_MULTIPLE}")
    print(f"elbow turns per torus orbit           = {elbow_turns_per_orbit:.13f}")
    print(f"required major/minor ratio R/b      = {ratio:.13f}")
    print(f"chosen tube/sphere radius b         = {b:.8f}")
    print(f"derived torus major radius R        = {R:.13f}")
    print(f"physical Analemma length            = {length_physical:.13f}")
    print(f"sphere great-circle circumference   = {sphere_circ:.13f}")
    print(f"tube cross-section circumference    = {tube_circ:.13f}")
    print(f"inner torus circumference           = {inner_circ:.13f}")
    print(f"inner circumference / Analemma L   = {inner_circ/length_physical:.13f}")
    print(f"E crossing tangent determinant      = {e_det:.13f} (nonzero = transverse)")
    print(f"W kissing tangent dot               = {w_dot:.13f} (1 = common tangent)")
    print(f"minimum spherical parameter speed   = {min_speed:.13f}")
    print(f"W_obble offset bound / b            = {midpoint_bound:.13f}")
    print("derivative finite-difference checks:")
    for h,e1err,e2err in derivative_errors:
        print(f"  h={h:.7g}: first={e1err:.3e}, second={e2err:.3e}")
    print("PASS: equal areas, E/W topology, regularity, radius equality, common sphere-roll/Analemma phase, 2× elbow lock, and 2:1 inner-circumference gearing")


if __name__=="__main__":
    main()

TAU=2*math.pi
b=.55
LA=13.269135039606383
delta=4.22369686421446
R=(1+delta)*b
K=2.6349970962925298

def beta(t): return K*np.sin(t)*np.cos(t)**2
def beta_p(t): return K*np.cos(t)*(1-3*np.sin(t)**2)
def beta_pp(t): return K*np.sin(t)*(9*np.sin(t)**2-7)
def an_frame(t):
    be=beta(t); bp=beta_p(t); bpp=beta_pp(t); p=2*t
    sb,cb,sp,cp=np.sin(be),np.cos(be),np.sin(p),np.cos(p)
    g=np.array([cb*cp,cb*sp,sb])
    eb=np.array([-sb*cp,-sb*sp,cb])
    ep=np.array([-sp,cp,0.])
    v1=eb*bp+ep*(2*cb)
    v2=eb*(bpp+4*sb*cb)+ep*(-4*bp*sb)+g*(-(bp*bp+4*cb*cb))
    speed=np.linalg.norm(v1)
    tangent=v1/speed
    h=np.cross(g,tangent)
    kg=np.dot(g,np.cross(v1,v2))/speed**3
    return g,tangent,h,kg

# Arc-length lookup for material Analemma phase.
nt=200001
ts=np.linspace(0,TAU,nt)
speeds=np.hypot(beta_p(ts),2*np.cos(beta(ts)))
arc=np.concatenate([[0],cumulative_trapezoid(speeds,ts)])
# Correct tiny cumulative-trapezoid error with analytic reference scale.
arc *= LA/arc[-1]

def an_at(psi):
    s=(delta*psi)%LA
    if s<1e-10 or s>LA-1e-10: s=0.
    t=np.interp(s,arc,ts)
    return an_frame(t)

def eq(t,side):
    if side=="r": return .55*(np.cos(2*t)+(3/11)*np.sin(3*t))
    return .60*(np.sin(3*t)+(1/6)*np.cos(5*t))
def bearing(t,side):
    kk=0 if side=="r" else .7
    return t+.11*(np.sin(2*t+kk)-np.sin(kk))+.03*(np.tanh(eq(t,side))-np.tanh(eq(0,side)))
def polar(t,side):
    north=side=="r"
    ap=.78+.20*np.tanh(eq(t,side))
    ph=bearing(t,side)+(0 if north else math.pi)
    return np.array([np.sin(ap)*np.cos(ph),np.sin(ap)*np.sin(ph),(1 if north else -1)*np.cos(ap)])
def follow(alpha,side):
    alpha=alpha%TAU
    t=brentq(lambda t:bearing(t,side)-alpha,0,TAU,xtol=1e-13)
    return polar(t,side)
def qmap(v,g,t,h,er,et,ez):
    return -er*np.dot(g,v)+et*np.dot(t,v)-ez*np.dot(h,v)
def poly_roots_ray(o,d):
    X=np.array([o[0]**2+o[1]**2,2*(o[0]*d[0]+o[1]*d[1]),d[0]**2+d[1]**2])
    Z=np.array([o[2]**2,2*o[2]*d[2],d[2]**2])
    A=np.polynomial.polynomial.polyadd(np.polynomial.polynomial.polyadd(X,Z),[R*R-b*b])
    P=np.polynomial.polynomial.polysub(np.polynomial.polynomial.polymul(A,A),4*R*R*X)
    roots=np.polynomial.polynomial.polyroots(P)
    roots=[float(x.real) for x in roots if abs(x.imag)<1e-7 and x.real>1e-8]
    roots.sort()
    return roots
def sample_hit(psi, elbow_mult=2):
    er=np.array([np.cos(psi),np.sin(psi),0.])
    et=np.array([-np.sin(psi),np.cos(psi),0.])
    ez=np.array([0.,0.,1.])
    g,t,h,kg=an_at(psi)
    Q=lambda v:qmap(v,g,t,h,er,et,ez)
    center=R*er
    sweep=psi
    A=follow(sweep,"r")
    B=follow(sweep,"q")
    pr=center+b*Q(A)
    pq=center+b*Q(B)
    dr=pq-pr
    direction=dr/np.linalg.norm(dr)
    ref=Q(ez)
    if abs(np.dot(ref,direction))>.9: ref=Q(np.array([0.,1.,0.]))
    u=ref-direction*np.dot(ref,direction)
    u=u/np.linalg.norm(u)
    v=np.cross(direction,u); v=v/np.linalg.norm(v)
    roll_phase=2*psi # derived common phase
    theta=elbow_mult*roll_phase
    elbow=u*np.cos(theta)+v*np.sin(theta)
    mid=(pr+pq)/2
    roots=poly_roots_ray(mid,elbow)
    if not roots: return None, roots
    lam=roots[0]
    hit=mid+lam*elbow
    inner=np.hypot(hit[0],hit[1])<R
    return (hit,inner,lam),roots

N=1401
res=[sample_hit(TAU*i/(N-1),2) for i in range(N)]
valid=[x[0] for x in res if x[0] is not None]
inner_count=sum(1 for x in valid if x[1])
jumps=[np.linalg.norm(valid[i][0]-valid[i-1][0]) for i in range(1,len(valid))]
len(valid),inner_count,len(valid)-inner_count,max(jumps),sum(j>.11 for j in jumps),np.percentile(jumps,[50,90,99])

I updated the instrument so sphere roll follows the Analemma material phase: two circuits per torus orbit, with elbow rotation fixed at twice that rate—four rotations per orbit.

**Validating behavior**

I updated the UI, documentation, README, and validator. Independent geometric testing confirms the new four-turn law, though first-hit discontinuities and some inner-wall jumps remain unresolved.

parts:
Agreed. The clean way to impose that equality is to define **sphere roll as the Analemma's material phase**, measured in the torus-co-rotating frame. Then there is one roll clock, not two competing ones.

The existing gear relation gives

\[
\frac{2\pi(R/b-1)b}{L_A}=2
\]

so the sphere completes exactly two Analemma circuits per torus orbit. Define the common phase as \(\phi_s=2\psi\). The minimum even elbow lock is therefore

\[
\boxed{\phi_e=2\phi_s=4\psi}
\]

That gives **four elbow rotations per torus orbit**. The \(R/b=5.223697\) axial-spin coefficient remains in the inertial-frame rolling equation, but it is not a separate phase clock. 

**The revised rotation law is committed to `main` and verified by repository readback.**

The instrument now has:
- Sphere roll / Analemma: **2 circuits per torus orbit**.
- Elbow: **4 rotations per torus orbit**, exactly 2× sphere roll.
- R/Q sweep: remains independently selectable from 1 to 6 turns, without changing the elbow ratio.
- Minimum shared return: one torus orbit.

I also removed the obsolete LCM calculation and updated the UI readouts and technical documentation.

**Numerical checks**
- Sphere-roll equality residual: \(4.4\times10^{-16}\).
- Elbow ratio residual: \(8.9\times10^{-16}\).
- All six R/Q sweep settings satisfy the one-orbit closure.
- JavaScript syntax and source assertions pass.

**One important remaining mechanical issue:** I reran a 1,401-phase Python reconstruction using exact torus-ray quartic roots. The new elbow law produces 592 inward-facing first hits and 809 outward-facing first hits. The previous law produced 546 inward-facing hits. The worst adjacent trace jump decreased from 2.735 to 2.251 model units, but the number of jumps above \(0.11b\) increased from 49 to 73.

So the new rotation lock is working mathematically, but the elbow still does not reliably trace the *inner* torus wall. I've clarified that distinction in the UI rather than allowing its sphere-contact diagnostic to imply otherwise.

**Files:** [Instrument](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/PUBLIC_SITE/instruments/whirligig/index.html) · [Derivation](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/PUBLIC_SITE/instruments/whirligig/ANALEMMA_CORRECTION_2026-10-21.md) · [Numerical validator](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/tools/whirligig_rq/validate_equal_area_analemma.py) · [Latest UI commit](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/commit/37daf1256c0f21a23e3686fd7f3d12d70cf8e286)

I have not verified completion of the GitHub Pages deployment or fetched the live page. The repository changes are confirmed; live publication is not yet confirmed.

The next mechanical problem is now sharply defined: **make the elbow's four-turn motion maintain continuous inward-facing contact**, without disturbing the common roll phase. <MemoryCite />

The existing gear relation gives

\[
\frac{2\pi(R/b-1)b}{L_A}=2
\]

so the sphere completes exactly two Analemma circuits per torus orbit. Define the common phase as \(\phi_s=2\psi\)\. The minimum even elbow lock is therefore

\[
\boxed{\phi_e=2\phi_s=4\psi}
\]

That gives **four elbow rotations per torus orbit**\. The \(R/b=5.223697\) axial-spin coefficient remains in the inertial-frame rolling equation, but it is not a separate phase clock.

**The revised rotation law is committed to `main` and verified by repository readback.**

The instrument now has\:

- Sphere roll / Analemma: **2 circuits per torus orbit**\.
- Elbow: **4 rotations per torus orbit**, exactly 2× sphere roll.
- R/Q sweep: remains independently selectable from 1 to 6 turns, without changing the elbow ratio.
- Minimum shared return: one torus orbit.

I also removed the obsolete LCM calculation and updated the UI readouts and technical documentation.

- Sphere-roll equality residual: \(4.4\times10^{-16}\)\.
- Elbow ratio residual: \(8.9\times10^{-16}\)\.
- All six R/Q sweep settings satisfy the one-orbit closure.

The elbow projects wherever its gimbal-directed ray intersects the torus. **No requirement that the hit be on the donut-hole-facing flank, the sphere-contacting surface, or any particular radial half of the torus.**

- We should not filter intersections by \(\rho<R\).
- The solver should report the actual projected point and handle multiple intersections and tangencies correctly.

thoughts.content: I’m recognizing that I treated “inner wall” and “inner radial contact” as hard geometric constraints. That made the elbow’s flank seem mandatory, but the specification never required that particular ray-intersection branch.

I conflated the named inner contact with a requirement that every elbow projection land on the hole-facing flank. That shortcut turned descriptive geometry into a hard constraint, even though the projection itself was unconstrained.

parts:
I think I can reconstruct the mistake. It was a chain of three conflations, each of which seemed reasonable in isolation but led to an unjustified conclusion.

**1. I conflated two different geometric relationships.**

The original construction names Donomphulon as a point on the inner torus circumference, associated with the sphere's nominated contact geometry. I carried that terminology over to the elbow, which is a separate moving component.

I implicitly assumed that because one part of the mechanism has an inner contact, the elbow must also contact that same side of the torus. That does not follow.

**2. I turned a descriptive phrase into a mathematical constraint.**

The implementation and notes used language such as *inner wall*. I translated that into the condition

\[
\rho < R
\]

where \(R\) is the torus major radius. That identifies the hole-facing radial flank. But it was my operational interpretation, not a requirement established by the specification.

**3. I confused a numerical problem with a mechanical requirement.**

The ray can intersect the torus more than once. Tangencies can appear or disappear, and a naïve first-root solver can jump between intersection branches. I wanted to eliminate those discontinuities by restricting the solver to one side.

That was the fundamental category error: I tried to solve a numerical continuity problem by imposing a physical constraint that the design never specified.

The distinction matters:

- **Geometry:** determines where the elbow projects.
- **Intersection mathematics:** determines how we calculate that projection, including multiple roots and tangencies.
- **Mechanical specification:** determines what the elbow is required to do.

I let the second dictate the third.

The correct approach is to preserve the specified mechanism, calculate its actual projection, and investigate any discontinuities as properties of that geometry. If the resulting trace has surprising behavior, that's something to understand, not something to prohibit in advance.

In short, I mistook a convenient assumption for a design necessity. That was my error. <MemoryCite />

parts:
The inner wall is intended to be the inside surface of the tube. But... your thinking is somewhat in line with something I've been thinking as well. There are multiple ways to accomplish the result we need, which is: 1) Polar curves capture the entirety of information defined by the input equations; that is, for either curve, its exact input equation can be reproduced directly from the curve. 2) The composite curve captures the totality of the information of both curves simultaneously. 3) The composite curve drawn on the inner surface of the torus should ideally be reverse-engineerable to produce an equation of the composite curve; ideally, a precise one, fully specifying the entirety of the curve (though approximately is acceptable, within some reasonable boundaries). 

So... what I've been thinking, to make the curve more well-behaved, and to force it to reconnect with itself after a finite (or even set) number of rotations, is something like this--
Construct a second crossbar that behaves exactly as the first, except 1) Its contact points with the curves are mirror-flipped... if the first crossbar intersects the northern curve in the eastern hemisphere, then the second intersects it in the western. 2) It swings about its trace of the two curves in the opposite direction, and it rotates in the opposite direction. 3) The elbow of the second crossbar (it's own elbow; neither mechanism is attached to the other anywhere). 4) Instead of tracing a composite curve, the pointer arm is anchored on the inside rim of the donut hole (and by virtue of that, it also intersects the center of the torus and the outer large circumference, 'slicing' the torus bagelwise). 

Constructed this way, I think what we'd have is the sphere rolling and wobbling such that it a) amplifies the wobble of the first crossbar, and b) keeps the projector arm pointed approximately on the outside (in the sense that you meant with the inside surface) of the torus. It would also (I think) force the curve to eventually reconnect with itself.

thoughts.content: I’m treating “inner wall” as the tube’s inside surface contacting the sphere, not merely the torus side facing the central opening. That distinction matters before I formalize the SAT rule or calculate anything.

I’m understanding the torus as a solid bagel-like body, with the sphere contacting its inward-facing tube surface. I’ll keep that interpretation separate from any inner radial flank or hollow-tube assumption when formalizing the geometry.

I’m treating the mirrored crossbar as a counter-rotating companion, not assuming it automatically creates closure. I’ll test whether symmetry preserves both parameterized input curves, since an unlabelled locus can lose phase and traversal information.

I’m distinguishing the physical trace from its parameterization. A composite path can encode both inputs only if it preserves phase, orientation, and branch identity; symmetry alone may otherwise erase essential information.

I’m viewing the second crossbar as a symmetry partner that can isolate or amplify antisymmetric motion. Mirror placement alone doesn’t guarantee wobble amplification; the phase, rotation sign, and chosen output difference determine that.

I’m separating three claims: physical amplification requires shared forces through the sphere; mathematical doubling requires differential output; exact closure requires commensurate phases. A torus trace must retain parameterization, orientation, and branch labels to recover the inputs.

I’m seeing the second arm as a moving coordinate reference: its opposite rotation can double relative phase, while the first trace carries shape. Exact decoding still requires synchronized parameterization, not just the unlabelled torus curve.

I’m treating the first bar as the data projector and the mirrored bar as a counter-rotating reference. Opposite motion can double relative phase, but physical amplification requires coupling through the shared sphere; otherwise it’s only differential measurement.

I’m treating the second pointer as a moving meridional reference, while the first remains the data projector. Opposite rotations can double relative phase, but mirror symmetry may reverse handedness, so global-coordinate signs must be defined explicitly.

thoughts.summary: Refined a dual mechanism geometry and tested linkage closure and amplification

parts:
I think there's a potentially important idea here. You're describing something more interesting than adding a second projector: **a conjugate mechanism that may turn the first mechanism's wobble into a useful, measurable relative motion, while providing a second geometric reference for reconstructing the trace.**

And I need to correct one thing from my last response: the intended target is still the tube's actual inside surface. What was unjustified was treating \(\rho<R\), the donut-hole-facing radial half, as an adequate definition of that surface. Those are not interchangeable descriptions without a proper geometric derivation.

## 1. The two mechanisms have complementary jobs

Here's how I'm interpreting the architecture.

<box border radius="lg" gap={3} padding={3}>
  <box gap={1}>
    <badge color="info">Mechanism A</badge>
    **Primary crossbar: information capture**
    - Samples the two polar curves.
    - Follows the prescribed motion of their contact points.
    - Carries its own independently rotating elbow.
    - Projects the composite curve onto the tube's inside surface.
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    <badge color="discovery">Mechanism B</badge>
    **Conjugate crossbar: reference and modulation**
    - Samples mirror-flipped contact points.
    - Swings and rotates in the opposite direction.
    - Has its own independent elbow.
    - Carries a pointer arm anchored at the inside rim of the donut hole.
    - Provides a moving reference that cuts through the torus rather than drawing a second composite curve.
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    **Shared element: the sphere**
    Both mechanisms participate in the same sphere's motion, but neither crossbar is physically attached to the other.
  </box>
</box>

The second mechanism could therefore be a kind of *counter-sweeper*: it doesn't duplicate the first mechanism's output; it provides a complementary way of observing and organizing the motion.

## 2. The wobble amplification idea has a mathematical basis

Consider a simplified east-west reflection:

\[
M(x,y,z)=(-x,y,z)
\]

Suppose the first mechanism has a wobble displacement

\[
\mathbf w_1=(w_x,w_y,w_z)
\]

and the second produces its mirror:

\[
\mathbf w_2=M\mathbf w_1
=(-w_x,w_y,w_z).
\]

Now consider their difference:

\[
\mathbf w_1-\mathbf w_2
=(2w_x,0,0).
\]

The east-west antisymmetric component is doubled. The mirror-symmetric components cancel.

That's a particularly interesting result. The two mechanisms could separate the sphere's motion into complementary modes:

- Their difference isolates and amplifies the mirror-antisymmetric wobble.
- Their sum isolates and amplifies the mirror-symmetric motion.

The opposite rotation may reinforce this effect in angular coordinates. If their angular phases are

\[
\theta_1(t)=\omega t,\qquad
\theta_2(t)=-\omega t,
\]

then their relative phase is

\[
\boxed{\Delta\theta(t)=2\omega t}.
\]

So the relative motion completes twice the angular excursion of either mechanism individually.

One qualification: this is an amplification of *relative motion*. If the mechanisms are merely independent tracers, it doesn't physically increase the first crossbar's wobble. If both interact kinematically with the same sphere, however, the sphere provides a shared coupling. That distinction will matter when we formalize the model.

## 3. The second pointer might solve a deeper problem

The pointer arm anchored on the inside rim of the donut hole is especially interesting.

If its motion defines a moving meridional reference through the torus, it gives us another way to describe the location of the primary projected trace.

For a standard ring torus, we can write a point on its surface as

\[
\mathbf T(u,v)=
\begin{pmatrix}
(R+a\cos v)\cos u\\
(R+a\cos v)\sin u\\
a\sin v
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Here:

- \(u\) describes position around the large circumference.
- \(v\) describes position around the tube's cross-section.

The inverse coordinate transformation is

\[
u=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)
\]

\[
v=\operatorname{atan2}
\left(z,\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-R\right).
\]

This is useful because the composite curve can then be represented as two functions:

\[
\boxed{C(t)=\big(u(t),v(t)\big)}.
\]

The primary mechanism generates the projected path. The secondary mechanism could provide a moving reference for its toroidal coordinates.

That might make the second mechanism useful not merely for stabilizing or redirecting the projector, but for making the composite curve easier to decode.

## 4. The three information requirements

I think these deserve to be treated as three separate mathematical tests.

| Requirement | What must be true |
|---|---|
| Polar curve reversibility | Each input curve preserves enough information to reconstruct its exact input equation. |
| Composite completeness | The combined trace uniquely represents the simultaneous state of both input curves. |
| Composite reversibility | The torus-surface trace can be converted back into a sufficiently precise equation. |

There is an important subtlety in the first requirement.

A geometric locus alone generally cannot reproduce its exact generating equation. Different parameterizations can describe the same geometric curve. So the object we need is not merely an unlabelled line. It is a **parameterized, oriented, phase-preserving curve**.

The same issue applies to the composite trace. If two different simultaneous states of R and Q project to the same point on the torus, the point alone cannot tell us which state produced it.

The second mechanism may help resolve that ambiguity by supplying another coordinate or reference. But we'll need to demonstrate that rather than assume it.

## 5. Will the second mechanism force closure?

This is the part where I would be cautious.

Mirror symmetry and counterrotation can make the trajectory more orderly, but they do not automatically guarantee finite closure.

For a system with several rotating phases, exact closure requires a common period \(T\) such that

\[
\omega_iT=2\pi n_i
\]

for every independent phase, with integer \(n_i\).

Equivalently, all independent frequency ratios must be rational.

The promising feature of your proposal is that the second mechanism need not introduce an independent clock. If its motions are exact mirror-conjugates of the first mechanism's motions, with reversed phase, then it adds no new independent frequency. It may actually make the combined system easier to phase-lock.

That is where I'd concentrate. We should derive the secondary motion from the primary motion and the reflection operation, rather than give it an independently chosen set of frequencies.

One further detail needs careful treatment: a mirror reflection already reverses handedness. Adding an explicitly opposite rotation can either produce the intended counterrotation or accidentally reverse the sign twice. We'll need to define both angular velocities in the same global coordinate frame.

---

## My current assessment

I see three potentially valuable functions emerging from the second mechanism:

1. **Differential amplification:** it makes certain components of the sphere's wobble more pronounced relative to the first mechanism.
2. **Geometric referencing:** its bagelwise pointer provides an independent moving reference for locating the primary projection on the torus.
3. **Phase regularization:** its mirror-conjugate motion may make the combined system easier to return to a precisely defined initial state.

The third is not yet proven, but it is a plausible design advantage.

I would not change the existing Whirligig implementation yet. The next step should be a mathematical model of both crossbars, their contact-point mappings, their signed rotations, and their shared sphere state. Then we can test three things computationally:

- Whether the secondary mechanism really amplifies the intended wobble modes.
- Whether the primary composite trace retains enough information to reconstruct R and Q.
- Whether the complete system has a finite exact return period.

**The most interesting possibility is that the second mechanism isn't just correcting the first. It may be providing the missing coordinate system that makes the first mechanism's output reversible.**

model_dil_v2.fallbackMarkdown:
I think there's a potentially important idea here. You're describing something more interesting than adding a second projector: **a conjugate mechanism that may turn the first mechanism's wobble into a useful, measurable relative motion, while providing a second geometric reference for reconstructing the trace.**

And I need to correct one thing from my last response: the intended target is still the tube's actual inside surface. What was unjustified was treating \(\rho<R\), the donut-hole-facing radial half, as an adequate definition of that surface. Those are not interchangeable descriptions without a proper geometric derivation.

## 1\. The two mechanisms have complementary jobs

Here's how I'm interpreting the architecture.

(Mechanism A)

**Primary crossbar: information capture**

- Samples the two polar curves.
- Follows the prescribed motion of their contact points.
- Carries its own independently rotating elbow.
- Projects the composite curve onto the tube's inside surface.

---

(Mechanism B)

**Conjugate crossbar: reference and modulation**

- Samples mirror-flipped contact points.
- Swings and rotates in the opposite direction.
- Has its own independent elbow.
- Carries a pointer arm anchored at the inside rim of the donut hole.
- Provides a moving reference that cuts through the torus rather than drawing a second composite curve.

---

**Shared element: the sphere**
Both mechanisms participate in the same sphere's motion, but neither crossbar is physically attached to the other.

The second mechanism could therefore be a kind of *counter-sweeper*\: it doesn't duplicate the first mechanism's output; it provides a complementary way of observing and organizing the motion.

## 2\. The wobble amplification idea has a mathematical basis

Consider a simplified east-west reflection\:

\[
M(x,y,z)=(-x,y,z)
\]

Suppose the first mechanism has a wobble displacement

\[
\mathbf w_1=(w_x,w_y,w_z)
\]

and the second produces its mirror\:

\[
\mathbf w_2=M\mathbf w_1
=(-w_x,w_y,w_z).
\]

Now consider their difference\:

\[
\mathbf w_1-\mathbf w_2
=(2w_x,0,0).
\]

The east-west antisymmetric component is doubled. The mirror-symmetric components cancel.

That's a particularly interesting result. The two mechanisms could separate the sphere's motion into complementary modes\:

- Their difference isolates and amplifies the mirror-antisymmetric wobble.
- Their sum isolates and amplifies the mirror-symmetric motion.

The opposite rotation may reinforce this effect in angular coordinates. If their angular phases are

\[
\theta_1(t)=\omega t,\qquad
\theta_2(t)=-\omega t,
\]

then their relative phase is

\[
\boxed{\Delta\theta(t)=2\omega t}.
\]

So the relative motion completes twice the angular excursion of either mechanism individually.

One qualification: this is an amplification of *relative motion*\. If the mechanisms are merely independent tracers, it doesn't physically increase the first crossbar's wobble. If both interact kinematically with the same sphere, however, the sphere provides a shared coupling. That distinction will matter when we formalize the model.

## 3\. The second pointer might solve a deeper problem

The pointer arm anchored on the inside rim of the donut hole is especially interesting.

If its motion defines a moving meridional reference through the torus, it gives us another way to describe the location of the primary projected trace.

For a standard ring torus, we can write a point on its surface as

\[
\mathbf T(u,v)=
\begin{pmatrix}
(R+a\cos v)\cos u\\
(R+a\cos v)\sin u\\
a\sin v
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Here\:

- \(u\) describes position around the large circumference.
- \(v\) describes position around the tube's cross-section.

The inverse coordinate transformation is

\[
u=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)
\]

\[
v=\operatorname{atan2}
\left(z,\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-R\right).
\]

This is useful because the composite curve can then be represented as two functions\:

\[
\boxed{C(t)=\big(u(t),v(t)\big)}.
\]

The primary mechanism generates the projected path. The secondary mechanism could provide a moving reference for its toroidal coordinates.

That might make the second mechanism useful not merely for stabilizing or redirecting the projector, but for making the composite curve easier to decode.

## 4\. The three information requirements

I think these deserve to be treated as three separate mathematical tests.

| Requirement | What must be true |
|--------|--------|
| Polar curve reversibility | Each input curve preserves enough information to reconstruct its exact input equation. |
| Composite completeness | The combined trace uniquely represents the simultaneous state of both input curves. |
| Composite reversibility | The torus-surface trace can be converted back into a sufficiently precise equation. |

There is an important subtlety in the first requirement.

A geometric locus alone generally cannot reproduce its exact generating equation. Different parameterizations can describe the same geometric curve. So the object we need is not merely an unlabelled line. It is a **parameterized, oriented, phase-preserving curve**\.

The same issue applies to the composite trace. If two different simultaneous states of R and Q project to the same point on the torus, the point alone cannot tell us which state produced it.

The second mechanism may help resolve that ambiguity by supplying another coordinate or reference. But we'll need to demonstrate that rather than assume it.

## 5\. Will the second mechanism force closure?

This is the part where I would be cautious.

Mirror symmetry and counterrotation can make the trajectory more orderly, but they do not automatically guarantee finite closure.

For a system with several rotating phases, exact closure requires a common period \(T\) such that

\[
\omega_iT=2\pi n_i
\]

for every independent phase, with integer \(n_i\)\.

Equivalently, all independent frequency ratios must be rational.

The promising feature of your proposal is that the second mechanism need not introduce an independent clock. If its motions are exact mirror-conjugates of the first mechanism's motions, with reversed phase, then it adds no new independent frequency. It may actually make the combined system easier to phase-lock.

That is where I'd concentrate. We should derive the secondary motion from the primary motion and the reflection operation, rather than give it an independently chosen set of frequencies.

One further detail needs careful treatment: a mirror reflection already reverses handedness. Adding an explicitly opposite rotation can either produce the intended counterrotation or accidentally reverse the sign twice. We'll need to define both angular velocities in the same global coordinate frame.

---

## My current assessment

I see three potentially valuable functions emerging from the second mechanism\:

1. **Differential amplification\:** it makes certain components of the sphere's wobble more pronounced relative to the first mechanism.
2. **Geometric referencing\:** its bagelwise pointer provides an independent moving reference for locating the primary projection on the torus.
3. **Phase regularization\:** its mirror-conjugate motion may make the combined system easier to return to a precisely defined initial state.

The third is not yet proven, but it is a plausible design advantage.

I would not change the existing Whirligig implementation yet. The next step should be a mathematical model of both crossbars, their contact-point mappings, their signed rotations, and their shared sphere state. Then we can test three things computationally\:

- Whether the secondary mechanism really amplifies the intended wobble modes.
- Whether the primary composite trace retains enough information to reconstruct R and Q.
- Whether the complete system has a finite exact return period.

**The most interesting possibility is that the second mechanism isn't just correcting the first. It may be providing the missing coordinate system that makes the first mechanism's output reversible.**

# Whirligig R/Q | Selectable equation adapters

**Status:** SANDBOXED / OPERATIONAL BROWSER INPUT LIBRARY (not a mathematical equivalence claim)  
**Date:** 2026-10-17  
**Browser implementation:** `PUBLIC_SITE/instruments/whirligig/index.html`  
**Implementation commit:** `0cf005a95051ce046be71a04f01c60a3a166ad1e`  
**Source engine reference:** `tools/whirligig_rq/README.md`, `whirligig.py`

## Design

Each input must provide an explicit dimensionless periodic *scalar representative* `f(λ)`, with λ ranging from zero to 2π and a periodic closed result. The instrument applies independent R and Q selection, R/Q **display** gain, and a Q sampling phase. The source's scalar value changes the spherical polar aperture through the existing bounded mapping, preserving opposite E/W hemispheres. It is **not** a universal invertible map from a field equation, metric, representation, wavefunction or solution space to a 3D curve.

Distinct input equations are mapped to the same sphere using an explicitly chosen adapter, not assumed to be isomorphic. Geometry coupling remains unchanged: independent source curves, simultaneous equal-fraction arc-length traversal, one variable-length crossbar, one perpendicular projecting elbow, minimum shared return clock, torus-wall Curvy Lisa output. The numerical comparison readout displays root-mean-square difference between the two **ungained scalar profile samples**, not an equation-isomorphism criterion or field-theory test.

## Catalog

| Code | Mathematical object | Specific selected closed representative | Epistemic scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| `harm_r` | synthetic harmonic R | cos(2λ)+(3/11)sin(3λ) | demonstration |
| `harm_q` | synthetic harmonic Q | sin(3λ)+(1/6)cos(5λ) | demonstration |
| `u1_phase` | U(1) relative phase | Re exp(i[λ+0.25 sin(2λ)]) | fixed-reference gauge phase; **not gauge invariant** |
| `su2_character` | SU(2) fundamental character | ½Tr diag(exp(iφ),exp(−iφ))=cos φ, φ=2λ+0.35sin λ | group path only; not an SU(2) Yang–Mills field |
| `su3_character` | SU(3) fundamental character | (1+2cos φ)/3, φ=2λ+0.25sin(3λ) | diagonal group path; not QCD dynamics or a Wilson loop |
| `gw_plus` | linearized vacuum GR wave | h₊/h₀=cos(2λ) | TT-gauge wave component, phase-normalized |
| `gw_cross` | linearized vacuum GR wave | h×/h₀=sin(2λ) | TT-gauge component, not gauge-independent complete spacetime |
| `schwarz_orbit` | Schwarzschild timelike circular geodesic | x/r₀=cos λ at equatorial r₀=8M | coordinate x projection, λ is **orbital phase**, not proper time |
| `schwarz_lapse` | Schwarzschild metric lapse | 10[√(1−2M/r(λ))−√(1−2/8)], r/M=8+1.5cos λ | prescribed radial scan, **not a geodesic** |
| `kerr_drag` | Kerr equatorial ZAMO frame dragging | ω(r)=2Ma/(r³+a²r+2Ma²); a/M=0.5; r/M=8+cos λ; f=ω(r)/ω(8M)−1 | prescribed radial scan, **not an orbit** |
| `qm_rabi` | two-level Schrödinger solution | H=(ℏΩ/2)σₓ, Pₑ=sin²(λ/2); 2Pₑ−1=−cos λ | ideal resonant system, λ=Ωt |
| `qm_spin` | spin-½ Larmor precession | H=(ℏω/2)σz; ⟨σₓ⟩=cos λ | ideal initial +x state, λ=ωt |
| `qm_coherent` | quantum harmonic oscillator coherent state | ⟨x⟩/A=cos(3λ) | selected expectation value, ωt=3λ |
| `qm_interference` | coherent two-energy-state superposition | interference factor cos(ΔEt/ℏ)=cos(3λ) | phase interference factor only, not the full probability density |

**Important gauge distinction:** the trace of a chosen group element is a class function under conjugation, but these chosen paths are *not* derived from a gauge connection integrated along physical closed spacetime loops. Do not present them as gauge-invariant Yang–Mills Wilson-loop measurements or solutions to the gauge field equations.

**Important GR distinction:** a selected metric is an exact gravitational solution in its stated idealized setting, but sampling one metric component along an arbitrarily imposed periodic radius does not automatically yield a geodesic or solve a new Einstein field equation. Only the stated Schwarzschild circular-orbit model uses a selected timelike geodesic.

**Important QM distinction:** phase, expectation value, and population probability are different objects. Each input explicitly states which is sampled. Do not equate scalar trace similarity with quantum-state equivalence.

## User interface

- Two independent selectors: **Equation R / East** and **Equation Q / West**, each containing all 14 profiles.
- Ten named pair presets for same-sector and cross-sector exploration.
- Swap R ↔ Q without claiming invariance of the crossbar/elbow output under swap.
- Equations and clear provenance/scope text visible adjacent to each selector.
- Original demonstration remains the default and reproduces the former coefficients when display gains are 0.55 and 0.60.
- Q sampling phase applies to the chosen Q input before the sphere projection.
- Source groups and formula labels are authored static data. No `eval` of user-supplied mathematics or dynamic execution of arbitrary expressions.
- Exported SVG reflects the selected composite elbow-tip trace.

## Verification and remaining work

The HTML file was independently read back from GitHub after its committed write. A stubbed JavaScript DOM/canvas test executed all 14 profiles on the R selector and all 14 on Q, tested all ten pair presets, independent swap, opposite hemisphere membership, numerical connector–elbow perpendicularity, and numerical torus-wall intersection existence. Maximum orthogonality residual over tested R/preset configurations was below 4.1e−16; all 1,651 samples in each tested configuration had an elbow–torus intersection. The **Q selector** likewise produced zero missing hits or E/W violations in the same baseline mechanical configuration.

These are executed geometry smoke tests **not** browser/visual-acceptance tests, and are not formal verification of the chosen mathematical adapters. Full browser usability, semantic mathematical review, and deployed ChatGPT Sites publication remain unverified.

Next steps: add optional parameter controls with domain/unit checking for each representative; standardize a serialized source specification compatible with the Python engine; separately validate higher-dimensional and nonperiodic solution branches without forcing fake closure; and test whether the experimental composite curves preserve source invariants beyond similar appearance.

## 2026-10-21 UPDATE: 42-profile unfiltered comparison library (supersedes 14-only summary)

The current browser implements the 14 earlier demonstration, gauge, GR, and QM profiles **plus 28 new mathematical representatives**. The selector groups now include **Best-known series (11)** and **Often overlooked series (17)**, alongside the original sector groups. The groups are editorial and exhaustive within this defined library; “best-known” and “often overlooked” are not objective rank, rarity, or significance assessments.

**Best-known:** Newtonian oscillator, Kepler ellipse, Maxwell vacuum wave, Fourier heat mode, Laplace disk harmonic, Schrödinger infinite-well eigenfunction scan, wave-equation standing mode, special-relativistic Lorentz factor, Planck spectrum, Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution, Fermi–Dirac occupation.

**Often overlooked:** Jacobi theta₃, Legendre P₄, Chebyshev T₅, Bessel J₀ (numerical quadrature), Clausen Cl₂ (truncated Fourier series), Re Li₂ (truncated power series), 2D Dirac Berry-curvature scan, Mathieu equation coefficient (not a Mathieu solution), KdV sech² soliton (periodic spatial scan, not a periodic traveling solution), sine–Gordon kink scan, Burgers viscous-shock profile scan, Morse potential, Lennard–Jones 12–6 potential, Kitaev-chain Bogoliubov band, Pöschl–Teller well, Fresnel C (numerical quadrature), U(1) Wilson phase for a **specified** family of fluxes.

The synthetic and physical examples are never declared automatically equivalent by curve appearance.

**Uncurated traversal:** `Next pair in series` deterministically walks all unordered pairs of the chosen set in lexicographic order, with a visible index; counts are 55 familiar, 136 overlooked, or 861 among all 42. This avoids auto-selecting outputs for beauty, similarity, or expected theory claims. Manual R/Q selection and original named pairs are preserved.

[L2]   "content": "# Whirligig / Analemma: terminology and functional reconstruction

**Date:** 2026-10-21. **Status:** SANDBOXED browser implementation, repository-published, **live Sites deployment unverified**.

## Direct user correction and provenance

The early records' **GrAnn / Great Annulum** was a mistaken term. The user intended an **Analemma**. That is a meaningful geometric correction, not a request to continue recovering a supposed self-intersecting annulum. Historical HsH files retain the wrong term for provenance and are superseded as operating specifications. The user also specifies that its purpose is to **lock all three sphere-rotation axes to the minimum shared closure and drive the single perpendicular elbow's revolution count from the common cycle**. The sphere is to roll on the **inner radial torus surface**.

For astronomical context only, the conventional solar analemma is the figure-eight locus of apparent solar declination versus equation of time at a fixed mean time of day. See the US Naval Observatory's [Equation of Time](https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/eqtime) explanation. The mechanical curve implemented here is a transparent **analemma-shaped spherical 1:2 harmonic candidate**, NOT a computed solar ephemeris or a claim that the original instrument uniquely requires this shape.

## Implemented 3D material contact curve

Let \(t\in[0,2\pi]\) run over one material Analemma circuit and \(A>0\) control its spherical aperture:

\[
G_A(t)=\frac{(-1,\ A\sin t,\ A(\sin2t+0.27\sin t))}{\|(-1,\ A\sin t,\ A(\sin2t+0.27\sin t))\|}.
\]

This is a closed self-intersecting curve on the **unit sphere** with unequal lobes. \(G_A(0)=G_A(\pi)=(-1,0,0)\), but the two branches have distinct tangent directions. Its full tangent, normal and signed geodesic curvature are computed from the curve's analytic derivatives, not fabricated from a torus drawing.

The older reconstruction's circular carrier has been replaced in both world and sphere-body displays. The UI labels it **Analemma**. Internal legacy variable names and research filenames may retain `grann` for implementation compatibility, but should not be mistaken for the user's corrected terminology.

## Inner-torus rolling and minimum return

Let the torus major radius be \(R\), both sphere radius and torus tube radius be \(b=a\), and \(\psi\) parameterize the torus-centerline orbit. Define unit radial \(e_r\), orbital tangent \(e_\phi\), vertical \(e_z\).

The selected point on the **inner** torus wall is \(Donomphulon=(R-b)e_r\). The separately named **outer** radial point remains \(P_{ivot}=(R+b)e_r\). Sphere center \(C=Re_r\). The selected contact offset is \(-b e_r\).

No-slip at this nominated inner contact:
\[
\dot C+\omega\times(-b e_r)=0.
\]

For the material Analemma, let \(s\) be **actual spherical arc length**, \(g=G_A(s)\), \(t=dg/ds\), \(h=g\times t\), and \(\kappa_g\) be signed geodesic curvature. The SO(3) lock is

\[
\mathcal Q(\psi)=[-e_r,\ e_\phi,\ -e_z]\,[g,t,h]^T,\qquad
\frac{ds}{d\psi}=\frac{R}{b}-1.
\]

This produces
\[
\boxed{\frac{\omega}{\dot\psi}=\frac{R}{b}e_z+
\left(\frac{R}{b}-1\right)\kappa_g(s)e_r}.
\]

The required \(+z\) rolling spin now has the **same sign as orbital travel**, unlike the earlier incorrect outer-wall model. The radial spin component rotates through **x and y** as the sphere goes around the torus, so all three spatial axes participate. ### Confirmed geometry and terminology

- **R** is a closed equation curve around the **north pole**, wholly in the northern hemisphere.
- **Q** is a closed equation curve around the **south pole**, wholly in the southern hemisphere.
- The Analemma is a separate closed spherical figure-eight. Its transverse self-crossing is at the **east equatorial pole** \(E=(1,0,0)\); its distinct self-tangential kiss is at the antipodal **west equatorial pole** \(W=(-1,0,0)\).
- The northern lobe winds around the north pole; the southern lobe winds around the south pole.
- One Analemma circuit means the complete two-lobed closed curve. The inner torus circumference is an even multiple of that complete length.
- Sphere radius equals torus tube minor radius: \(b=a\), so the sphere great-circle circumference equals the tube cross-section circumference.

The historical source gives the self-crossing and antipodal self-tangency relationship; the E/W versus N/S placement and the equal-area condition above are the user's later explicit geometric refinements.

### Equal-area curve family and solved shape

On the unit sphere, define

\[
\beta(t)=k\sin t\cos^2t,\qquad \phi(t)=2t,
\]

\[
G(t)=\bigl(\cos\beta\cos\phi,\;\cos\beta\sin\phi,\;\sin\beta\bigr),
\quad 0\le t<2\pi.
\]

The northern lobe is \(0<t<\pi\); the southern lobe is \(\pi<t<2\pi\). The equal-area interpretation used here is that the **combined two-lobe area** equals the remaining equatorial area. Thus each lobe encloses \(\pi b^2\), both lobes enclose \(2\pi b^2\), and the complement also has area \(2\pi b^2\).

The area equation is

\[
2\int_0^\pi\left[1-\sin\left(k\sin t\cos^2t\right)\right]dt=\pi.
\]

Its first regular root is

\[
\boxed{k=2.63499709629253}.
\]

The maximum lobe latitude is \(58.11000154^\circ\). At E, the two branch tangent vectors in local azimuth/latitude components are proportional to \((2,k)\) and \((2,-k)\), so the crossing is transverse. At W, both tangent vectors are proportional to \((2,0)\), while their second-order latitude curvature has opposite sign, giving the intended tangential kiss. The curve is regular; its minimum parameter speed on the unit sphere is greater than 1.

### Length and gearing

The full material length is

\[
L_A=b\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{\beta'(t)^2+4\cos^2\beta(t)}\,dt
=13.26913503960638\,b.
\]

For the minimum positive even multiple, the inner torus circumference contains two full Analemma circuits:

\[
2\pi(R-b)=2L_A,\qquad
\boxed{R/b=5.22369686421446}.
\]

The browser therefore derives the major radius from the tube/sphere radius. At the retained reference scale \(b=a=0.55\):

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---:|
| Sphere and tube radius | 0.55 |
| Sphere great-circle / tube cross-section circumference | 3.45575191895 |
| Full physical Analemma length | 7.29802427178 |
| Torus major radius \(R\) | 2.87303327532 |
| Inner torus circumference | 14.59604854357 |
| Inner circumference / full Analemma length | 2 exactly, within numerical tolerance |

Changing the scale control changes \(a=b\) and derives \(R\) proportionally, preserving the equal circumferences and two-circuit gear ratio. The old independent major-radius slider is removed because it allowed the gear constraint to be broken.

### R/Q aperture and W_obble centering

The R/Q polar aperture adapter is \(a_{RQ}=0.78+0.20\tanh(f)\) radians. R is placed around \(+z\) and Q around \(-z\), with opposite azimuths at a common meridional sweep. The aperture gain bounds the normalized crossbar-midpoint offset by \(\sin(0.20)=0.19866933\); the default harmonic pair's sampled maximum is about \(0.0931\) sphere radii. Across the 84 one-port profile configurations tested, the largest sampled offset is \(0.12914\) sphere radii. The azimuth/equation mapping remains an explicit representation choice, not a derived field equation.

The browser computes the Analemma tangent, normal, and signed geodesic curvature analytically, transports its material point by numerical arc-length inversion, and keeps the existing inner selected-contact no-slip relation. The minimum even winding is now fixed at two full Analemma circuits per torus orbit; the elbow turns remain the LCM of that count and the R/Q sweep count.

Equal area is the chosen geometric balance condition. It has **not** been proven to globally minimize angular acceleration or jerk over all possible spherical figure-eight curves. A separate constrained smoothness optimization would be needed to establish that stronger claim. Equal-radius contact remains nonisolated, so the model still certifies only the nominated contact, not global no-slip across the full contact locus.

This is a working, configurable **two-equation** mechanism drawn from the historical R/Q / Great Annulum / W_obble / W_iggle / Curvy_Lisa description, together with the archived continuous Navier–Stokes Whirligig Python predecessor. It generates equation curves on a sphere, carries them inside a rolling ball constrained by a torus, uses two genuine orthogonal gimbal hinges to select curve endpoints, constructs the R–Q crossbar and a rotation-minimizing plane perpendicular to it, then intersects a rotating pen ray with the **actual torus quartic** to generate Curvy_Lisa.

## Input equation adapters

Two independent specs are supplied as `R` and `Q` in a JSON file. Every adapter records its representation choice, physical units remain those of the caller, and original numerical coordinates are preserved apart from the sphere carrier. **No universal faithful parameterization exists for arbitrary symbolic equations without specifying a solution branch, observables, and a parameter interval.** Accordingly the tool supports:

|---|---|---|---|
| `expression` | `0.5*cos(2*t)+0.1*sin(5*t)` | Scalar function encoded reversibly in sphere latitude; azimuth is `t` | Functions must be finite on the interval. Periodicity tested, not fabricated |

## Exact selected-contact rolling law

Let the torus have major radius `R` and tube/minor radius `a`. Let the sphere have radius `b<a` and travel on a center circle of radius

\[
\rho=R+a-b,\qquad C(\psi)=\rho(\cos\psi,\sin\psi,0).
\]

The selected contact on the outer equator is

\[
P(\psi)=(R+a)(\cos\psi,\sin\psi,0)=C+b\mathbf e_r.
\]

For rolling without slip at this **isolated chosen point**, the laboratory angular velocity obeys

\[
\boldsymbol\omega=-\frac{\rho}{b}\dot\psi\mathbf e_z,
\quad \dot C+\boldsymbol\omega\times(b\mathbf e_r)=0.
\]

Define the Great-Annulum body contact angle

\[
\gamma(\psi)=\frac{R+a}{b}\psi.
\]

Let `W(ψ)` be the orthonormal world frame `(e_r,e_phi,e_z)` and `B(γ)` the body-frame triad `(r_annulus,t_annulus,n_annulus)`. The **actual orientation** is

\[
\mathcal Q(\psi)=W(\psi)B(\gamma)^T\in SO(3).
\]

`P=C+Q b r_annulus` is tested point by point. A whole-revolution orientation closes when the contact gearing `g=(R+a)/b` is integral. The historical *even multiple* condition is satisfied by choosing `g=6` by default:

- `R=1.6`, `a=0.55`, `b=(R+a)/6=0.358333...`, `rho=1.791666...`.
- A five-point fourth-order finite-difference check of the no-slip velocity converges to zero under grid refinement, while the underlying analytic identity is exact.
- With `b=a` (the originally described limiting sphere size), ball and torus tube share a nonisolated meridional contact set. The program **can render that mode** when `allow_degenerate_contact=true`, but explicitly does **not certify unique-contact rolling**; imposing no slip at every contact point would be overconstrained.

## Gimbal, connector and pen

The input R endpoint is acted on by an internal `Ry(pitch)` hinge; the Q endpoint by an independent `Rx(roll)` hinge. Their axes are perpendicular **by exact construction**. Hinge angles use integer-period rotations with optional sinusoidal modulations. The sphere's physical `SO(3)` rotation is separate from these **internal coordinate controls**. The two endpoints are transported into the lab frame with the exact `Q(ψ)` orientation above.

`W_obble=(R_world+Q_world)/2` is the connector midpoint, and `W_iggle` is the plane perpendicular to the connector. A minimal-rotation Bishop frame supplies its two orthonormal axes. The pen rotates in that plane. Its **first forward** intersection with the torus is found by solving the torus implicit quartic and selecting its smallest positive real root, not by approximating a torus-looking curve.

Optional `align_source_anchors` rotates one source curve **by a single rigid SO(3) alignment**, mapping an off-phase point and tangent on Q to a point and tangent on R. This is a transparent representation intervention, **not an isomorphism proof**, and it is logged with the alignment matrix and both residuals.

An optional Bishop-holonomy correction adjusts the pen's phase around the full circuit. The correction is recorded, and may be disabled: the program does not silently assert that an uncompensated trace must close.

## Results and automatic smoothness search

The `--search` scan varies **four even annulum gear ratios**, pen rotation rates, and independently chosen gimbal rotations. It preserves **all sixty** ranked candidates in `ranked_candidates.json`, including failures; it also saves the selected best candidate's full reproducible arrays, metrics and precision geometry figures. - nondegenerate sphere/tube clearance;

**Date:** 2026-10-21. **Status:** SANDBOXED browser implementation, repository-published, **live Sites deployment unverified**.

## Direct user correction and provenance

The early records' **GrAnn / Great Annulum** was a mistaken term. The user intended an **Analemma**. That is a meaningful geometric correction, not a request to continue recovering a supposed self-intersecting annulum. Historical HsH files retain the wrong term for provenance and are superseded as operating specifications. The user also specifies that its purpose is to **lock all three sphere-rotation axes to the minimum shared closure and drive the single perpendicular elbow's revolution count from the common cycle**. The sphere is to roll on the **inner radial torus surface**.

For astronomical context only, the conventional solar analemma is the figure-eight locus of apparent solar declination versus equation of time at a fixed mean time of day. See the US Naval Observatory's [Equation of Time](https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/eqtime) explanation. The mechanical curve implemented here is a transparent **analemma-shaped spherical 1:2 harmonic candidate**, NOT a computed solar ephemeris or a claim that the original instrument uniquely requires this shape.

## Implemented 3D material contact curve

Let \(t\in[0,2\pi]\) run over one material Analemma circuit and \(A>0\) control its spherical aperture:

\[
G_A(t)=\frac{(-1,\ A\sin t,\ A(\sin2t+0.27\sin t))}{\|(-1,\ A\sin t,\ A(\sin2t+0.27\sin t))\|}.
\]

This is a closed self-intersecting curve on the **unit sphere** with unequal lobes. \(G_A(0)=G_A(\pi)=(-1,0,0)\), but the two branches have distinct tangent directions. Its full tangent, normal and signed geodesic curvature are computed from the curve's analytic derivatives, not fabricated from a torus drawing.

The older reconstruction's circular carrier has been replaced in both world and sphere-body displays. The UI labels it **Analemma**. Internal legacy variable names and research filenames may retain `grann` for implementation compatibility, but should not be mistaken for the user's corrected terminology.

## Inner-torus rolling and minimum return

Let the torus major radius be \(R\), both sphere radius and torus tube radius be \(b=a\), and \(\psi\) parameterize the torus-centerline orbit. Define unit radial \(e_r\), orbital tangent \(e_\phi\), vertical \(e_z\).

The selected point on the **inner** torus wall is \(Donomphulon=(R-b)e_r\). The separately named **outer** radial point remains \(P_{ivot}=(R+b)e_r\). Sphere center \(C=Re_r\). The selected contact offset is \(-b e_r\).

No-slip at this nominated inner contact:
\[
\dot C+\omega\times(-b e_r)=0.
\]

For the material Analemma, let \(s\) be **actual spherical arc length**, \(g=G_A(s)\), \(t=dg/ds\), \(h=g\times t\), and \(\kappa_g\) be signed geodesic curvature. The SO(3) lock is

\[
\mathcal Q(\psi)=[-e_r,\ e_\phi,\ -e_z]\,[g,t,h]^T,\qquad
\frac{ds}{d\psi}=\frac{R}{b}-1.
\]

This produces
\[
\boxed{\frac{\omega}{\dot\psi}=\frac{R}{b}e_z+
\left(\frac{R}{b}-1\right)\kappa_g(s)e_r}.
\]

The required \(+z\) rolling spin now has the **same sign as orbital travel**, unlike the earlier incorrect outer-wall model. The radial spin component rotates through **x and y** as the sphere goes around the torus, so all three spatial axes participate. This is mathematically an **inner selected-contact** constraint, not global no-slip over the nonisolated \(b=a\) contact locus.

Let \(L_G(A)\) be the true spherical arclength of one material Analemma. One torus orbit moves through \(2\pi(R/b-1)\) of material arc length. The model searches for the **smallest positive even** winding count \(n\), subject to its openly stated admissible aperture \(0<A\le2\), satisfying

\[
n L_G(A)=2\pi\left(\frac{R}{b}-1\right).
\]

With \(R=1.65\), \(b=0.55\), the minimum is \(n=2\), numerical \(A\approx0.935206924\), and \(L_G\approx2\pi\). This is *minimal within this declared family and bounded aperture*, not a universal minimum across all possible analemmas.

The R/Q moving sweep plane still intersects each source curve separately. The one and only perpendicular elbow is phase-locked to \(\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)\), where \(m\) is the chosen integer R/Q sweep count per torus orbit. No extra projector and no independent elbow-turn slider.

### Numerical transport detail

The current browser integrates Analemma arclength with composite Simpson quadrature, inverts its monotone \(s(t)\) table with a bracket and a local Newton/Simpson refinement, and advances the material track by actual arc length. This avoids piecewise-linear angular-velocity kinks in the first implementation.

Executed independent tests at finite-difference steps \(0.012, 0.006, 0.003, 0.0015, 0.00075\) orbital radians gave maximum selected-contact slip discrepancies approximately \(0.03109, 0.00843, 0.00215, 0.000542, 0.000136\), respectively. These converge close to the expected \(O(h^2)\), rather than only repeating the analytic identity used in the constructor. Full orientation closure residual about \(1.1\times10^{-15}\), and length/cycle return residual about \(4.6\times10^{-13}\).

## Equation-to-curve issue and remedy

The previous source mapping squeezed both R and Q into narrow hemisphere bands:

```text
old polar aperture: 0.48 + 0.20 tanh(display_gain * f(lambda))
current aperture:   0.78 + 0.58 tanh(display_gain * f(lambda))
```

These are explicit geometric *representation choices*, not newly derived equation identities. Angles remain between \(0.20\) and \(1.36\) radians, keeping the chosen half-sphere assignment. The more expressive mapping allows changing source equations to produce visibly different connector and torus-wall traces.

A fourth browser panel now compares **the previous and current actual torus-wall intersection curves at the same orbital parameters**, and displays RMS and maximum world-distance change in model units and tube-radius percentage. The previous trace appears dimly behind the current trace, both in the same torus coordinate system. Nothing is auto-reselected for visual beauty.

**Expected exact duplicates:** distinct underlying equations can define the same sampled scalar representative (e.g. \(\cos\lambda\) for both an ideal spin-precession expectation and a selected circular-orbit coordinate). If selected in the same input port under identical settings, they should produce the same mapped trace. The comparison panel explicitly calls out zero difference. **The instrument still does not establish physical equivalence** of two theories.

## Output continuity, no curation

The torus trace is defined by the first forward intersection of the **single elbow ray** with the implicit torus surface. Geometrically valid wall intersections do not imply continuity of the selected-first-hit branch. The application now reports counts of adjacent-step displacements greater than \(0.20b\) and the largest step, without smoothing or deleting events. In one default 1,401-point run, 30 adjacent steps exceeded \(0.11\) model units and the largest step was about \(0.347\). These are *discontinuity candidates*; determining whether they are true root-branch transitions or very rapid continuous motion requires an additional adaptive-step/root-continuation audit.

**Unresolved:** a mathematical derivative mapping \(Q\text{ wrt }R\), complete arbitrary-field invertibility, real-browser visual acceptance, live-site deployment, and global no-slip at \(b=a\). The spherical analemma is one explicit model of the user-intended track, not a claim of recovered solar-ephemeris mechanics.
